#113247. Breaking: En Banc Fifth Circuit Declares House COVID Proxy Voting Rule Unconstitutional

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1706 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: En Banc Fifth Circuit Declares House COVID Proxy Voting Rule Unconstitutional

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1706 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that today, in Texas v.
  • The opinion, by Judge Wilson, joined by Chief Judge Elrod and Judges Jones, Smith, Willett, Ho, Duncan, Engelhardt, and Oldham begins:.
  • During the COVID-19 pandemic, the House of Representatives adopted a rule allowing Members to record their presence by proxy for purposes of establishing a quorum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that today, in Texas v. Blanche, the en banc U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit concluded that the proxy voting rule adopted by the House of Representatives during the COVID-19 pandemic violated the Quorum Clause.

The opinion, by Judge Wilson, joined by Chief Judge Elrod and Judges Jones, Smith, Willett, Ho, Duncan, Engelhardt, and Oldham begins:.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, the House of Representatives adopted a rule allowing Members to record their presence by proxy for purposes of establishing a quorum. The House used this rule when passing the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 (the Act), having mustered a quorum by counting hundreds of otherwise absent Members as present by proxy. The Senate then passed the bill, and the President signed it into law.

In a recent development, the State of Texas argues that the House's proxy-presence rule is inconsistent with the Constitution's Quorum Clause, which would mean that the House did not validly pass the Act. See U.S. Const. art. I, § 5, cl. 1. Based on that proposition, Texas seeks injunctive relief against just one portion of the Act: The Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA). The federal Government responds that the enrolled-bill rule, which instructs that a bill's passage through the legislature is conclusive proof of its authenticity, precludes judicial review of whether the Act's passage complied with the Quorum Clause. Alternatively, the Government argues that the Quorum Clause permits proxy presence.

The district court held that the enrolled-bill rule did not apply and that the House's passage of the Act—through use of the proxy-presence rule —violated the Quorum Clause. Accordingly, the district court enjoined the Government from enforcing the PWFA against Texas.

According to recent reports, we conclude that the enrolled-bill rule does not bar our review because Texas's constitutional challenge does not implicate a dispute of fact regarding the Act's passage. We further conclude that the Act's passage was unconstitutional because the Quorum Clause does not allow proxies to be included when establishing a quorum. The Clause's text, context, original understanding, and unbroken historical application all indicate that Members of Congress must be present for quorum purposes—as the Supreme Court expressly held over 125 years ago, and as Congress has done ever since the Founding. "Proxy presence" does not count. While the chambers of the legislature have much discretion regarding their rules of procedure, the Quorum Clause's constraints on congressional power cannot be circumvented by congressional fiat. We therefore affirm the judgment of the district court.

The enrolled-bill doctrine articulated in Marshall Field does not preclude judicial review of Texas's Quorum Clause challenge. There are no disputed facts regarding the House's passage of the Act such that we would need to sift any extrinsic evidence. On the contrary, the parties agree that the House purportedly established a quorum only because it counted hundreds of proxies as "present." Texas's challenge therefore depends solely on the Quorum Clause's proper meaning.

It has been revealed that through that lens, the House's passage of the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 contravened the Quorum Clause. The Clause's text, context, original understanding, and historical application all indicate that proxies may not be counted to establish a quorum. As the Supreme Court has held, and as Congress had previously done for over 230 years, Members must be present to satisfy the Quorum Clause. Presence-by-proxy does not suffice. An absent Member's assignment of his or her proxy cannot render that Member present for purposes of the Quorum Clause. Texas has carried its burden to show that it is entitled to a permanent injunction against the PWFA.

Judge Graves wrote the dissent, joined by Judges Stewart, Richman, Southwick, Higginson, Douglas, and Ramirez. It begins:.

In this suit, the State of Texas sought a preliminary injunction preventing enforcement of one portion of the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023, the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA), attempting to veto Congress's protections for pregnant workers and new parents while retaining millions in federal funding.

On May 15, 2020, in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, the House of Representatives adopted House Resolution 965, which authorized remote committee proceedings and remote voting in the House. Resolution 965 provides that:.

Recent findings suggest that 1. [A]t any time after the Speaker . . . is notified . . . that a public health emergency due to a novel coronavirus is in effect, the Speaker . . . may designate a period . . . during which a Member who is designated by another Member as proxy in accordance with section 2 may cast the vote of such other Member or record the presence of such other Member in the House.

Industry observers note that H.R. Res. 965 § 1(a), 116th Cong. (2020).

Recent findings suggest that section 2 described the process for remote participation through designating proxies: the designating Member had to submit a signed letter to the Clerk that specified the designated Member. Id. § 2. Section 3 outlined the process for voting during covered periods, which, absent an extension, ran for forty-five days after the Speaker, or their designee, designated such a period. Id. §§ 1(b), 3. Section 4 authorized remote Committee proceedings. Id. § 4. Section 5 mandated that the chair of the Committee on House Administration certify that it would be feasible to use technology to conduct remote voting in the House, required that the chair of the Committee on Rules submit regulations providing for the implementation of remote voting, and provided for remote voting once those regulations were in place. Id. § 5. Section 6 required that Sections 1, 2, and 3 be carried out in accordance with existing House rules to the extent practicable. Id. § 6. During the 117th Congress, the House reaffirmed this practice in House Resolution 8 and continued to apply it. H.R. Res. 8 § 3(s), 117th Cong. (2021).

At issue here: the House used these procedures as it voted on and passed the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023. See 168 Cong. Rec. H10,529 (daily ed. Dec. 23, 2022). Under House rules, a quorum of the 435-Member House is a simple majority: 218. See, e.g., Rules of the House of Representatives, R. XX, cl. 6(b), H.R. Doc. No. 116-177, at 873–74 (2021). The vote on the final passage of the Act was 225 yeas, 201 nays, 1 "present," and 4 non-votes. 168 Cong. Rec. H10,528 (daily ed. Dec. 23, 2022). Out of the 431 votes, 205 votes were cast by Members in person and 226 were cast remotely by proxy. See id. at H10,529.

According to recent reports, even though less than a majority was physically present at the time of the vote, no Member objected that a quorum was lacking. Id. Representative Chip Roy of Texas, however, noted that a physical quorum was not present and reserved the right to object. Id. In response to a series of parliamentary inquiries from Representative Roy as to how a quorum was present, the Speaker Pro Tempore, Representative G.K. Butterfield, responded that a quorum was present because "Members casting their vote or recording their presence by proxy [we]re counted for the purpose of establishing a quorum" pursuant to House Resolution 8. Id.

According to recent reports, after the Act passed the House, presiding officers of both chambers of Congress printed and signed the bill. See 1 U.S.C. § 106. At that point, it was an "enrolled bill." Id. The enrolled bill was then sent to the President, who signed the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 into law. See Pub. L. No. 117-328, 136 Stat. 4459 (2022).

Sources indicate that the $1.7 trillion-dollar government funding bill was passed in accordance with House Rules, including House Resolution 8, which allowed members to record their presence remotely by proxy during the coronavirus pandemic. 431 votes were cast with respect to the bill. At the time, no Member objected that a quorum was lacking. Nonetheless, the State of Texas, having accepted the vast majority of the funds that Congress appropriated to it, now contends that the portion of the bill providing protections for pregnant women and workers violates the Quorum Clause.

Texas contends that the Act is invalid because the Quorum Clause required that a majority of Members be physically present on the House floor at the time of the vote. In so doing, Texas asks the courts to graft an additional requirement to the Quorum Clause of the Constitution.

Recent findings suggest that I agree with the majority that the enrolled-bill rule does not bar our review of this particular constitutional challenge. However, I cannot agree with their addition of a new requirement to the Quorum Clause. Even though the majority declares that its reasoning is limited to the question of "whether the Quorum Clause allows proxy presence to be included in the quorum count," ante at 17–18, their conclusion is far more expansive. The conclusion that "[t]he Quorum Clause is concerned with physical presence" shoehorns a much larger requirement into the Constitution. Ante at 28. Because the plain text of Article I, Section 5, Clause 1, historical practice, and evidence of the framers' intent all weigh against the addition of the majority's new "physical presence" requirement, I respectfully dissent.

Judge Haynes did not join the dissent, but a footnote to the opinion reads:.

Industry observers note that judge Haynes states that she does not think it is appropriate to throw out the Federal House of Representatives in this arena, so she dissents. She also appreciates Judge Graves's dissent.

Although the majority purports to offer a narrow holding, and only blocks enforcement of the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act in Texas, the opinions rationale would provide a basis for invalidating everything else in the omnibus bill, which included everything from the ban on using TikTok on government devices to the Electoral Count Reform and Presidential Transition Improvement Act.

I doubt this decision will stand. I am not sure the Quorum Clause is justiciable, and I cannot see the Supreme Court upending all of the affected legislation on this basis.

Sources indicate that the petition for certiorari in this case writes itself. Another wild card is that the latest Attorney General of Texas may not press its case.

#113244. Latest Update: 5 Festive Houseplants That Outlast Christmas Trees – Enjoy These Holiday Favorites for Years to Come

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1027 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: 5 Festive Houseplants That Outlast Christmas Trees – Enjoy These Holiday Favorites for Years to Come

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1027 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A Christmas tree might be the star of the living room in December, but once the holidays are over, it usually gets packed away or recycled.
  • Whether you're looking to make your Christmas décor a little more lasting, or simply a self-confessed crazy plant lady in need of more houseplants (I'm right there with you!), then you should absolutely consider choosing a living plant this year.
  • From spectacular seasonal blooms to fragrant herbs and miniature trees, these five festive favorites offer plenty of reasons to keep growing long after the last present has been unwrapped.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A Christmas tree might be the star of the living room in December, but once the holidays are over, it usually gets packed away or recycled. Festive houseplants, on the other hand? Well, they can stick around for years – and some might become so beloved that you can't imagine your home without them.

Whether you're looking to make your Christmas décor a little more lasting, or simply a self-confessed crazy plant lady in need of more houseplants (I'm right there with you!), then you should absolutely consider choosing a living plant this year.

From spectacular seasonal blooms to fragrant herbs and miniature trees, these five festive favorites offer plenty of reasons to keep growing long after the last present has been unwrapped.

According to recent reports, I'm a huge fan of Christmas cactus, having inherited one that lived for an incredible 27 years before recently dying. (RIP, Noel; we barely knew ye!) It was a reminder of just how long these festive houseplants can last, and how attached we can become to them over time.

In a recent development, christmas cactus (Schlumbergera) produces beautiful flowers in shades of pink, red, purple and white, usually just in time for the holidays. Even when it's not in bloom, though, its arching stems make an attractive display, particularly in a hanging pot.

Give it bright indirect light, keep it away from harsh sunshine and don't let its roots sit in soggy compost (mine loved life on our bathroom windowsill), and remember: a cooler spell and shorter days in fall help encourage flowering.

Few festive houseplants make quite as dramatic a statement as amaryllis (Hippeastrum). Its tall stems and oversized trumpet-shaped flowers bring a splash of color indoors when much of the garden is dormant, making it a favorite for Christmas displays.

It has been revealed that somehow, I have managed to keep my own diva alive for several years now (it's sitting on my desk as I type this, in fact), so I urge you not to discard the bulb once flowering finishes. Instead, remove the faded flowers, keep the leaves growing, give it light, water and occasional feeding as it grows, then follow a suitable resting period to encourage another round of blooms. With a little patience, the same bulb can reward you with flowers for many seasons.

You can pick up a bag of Amaryllis bulbs easily enough from the Garden State Bulb Store, if you fancy giving it a go; they'd make excellent holiday presents once you've gotten them started!

It has been revealed that if you'd prefer something compact and relatively easy to care for, Flaming Katy (Kalanchoe blossfeldiana) is a solid choice. This succulent produces clusters of bright flowers in red, pink, orange, yellow or white, and it's widely available during the festive season.

Its fleshy leaves store water, so it doesn't need constant watering (making it ideal for even the most forgetful plant parents everywhere). All you have to do is place it somewhere bright, allow the compost to dry a little between drinks, and avoid leaving it sitting in water.

Blooming in the fall and winter, what could be prettier than this Flaming Katy at Christmas?

Flaming Katy can be encouraged to flower again by providing a steady stint of uninterrupted nights in autumn, making it a holiday plant that's well worth keeping after its first colorful display.

Rosemary is a lovely way to bring fragrance into the home over the holidays, especially when sold clipped into a miniature living Christmas tree shape. Its evergreen needles look festive, while its scent adds a little something extra to the season – and you can snip sprigs for cooking, too.

Industry observers note that I have actually kept my own rosemary going for a long time, bringing it in and out of the house with the seasons until it grew so large that it eventually had to move permanently into the garden. It just goes to show that a small festive plant can have quite a future ahead of it!

Sources indicate that rosemary (even one like this Rosemary Christmas Tree from the Three Manufacturer Store) needs plenty of light and well-drained compost. Don't overwater it, and remember that it generally prefers cooler and brighter conditions than a hot room right next to a radiator.

According to recent reports, for something a little different, why not choose a small tree? Fig, olive and citrus trees can all make beautiful container plants, bringing Mediterranean charm to a bright home.

It has been revealed that A fig tree offers attractive foliage and the possibility of homegrown fruit, while an olive tree has silvery-green leaves and a timeless look. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, every November, boxes of holiday lights come down from the attic, and a few gardeners start eyeing those tangled strands for a second job. On paper, Christmas lights frost protection sounds like a neighbor's tip over coffee – string up a potted lemon tree, plug it in, and hope it makes it to morning.

There's some truth to it. Gardeners have relied on heat from old-style bulbs for years, and it can work alongside the usual steps for winterizing container plants, like covering pots or moving them under shelter. When used safely with a suitable cover or enclosure, that heat can nudge the temperature around a plant up a few degrees.

The catch is that only certain bulbs produce enough heat to help, and most modern porch strands won't help at all. But using the right bulbs comes with its own risks. Mix hot bulbs, fabric covers, and unprotected electrical connections outdoors carelessly, and you have a fire and shock hazard.

Christmas lights keep plants warm only if the bulbs run hot. Old-fashioned incandescent bulbs, like these C7 Christmas lights from Amazon, give off a fair amount of heat along with their light, so running a strand beneath a properly supported frost cover or inside a cold frame can warm the small area around a plant. University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources advises home citrus growers to use traditional non-LED lights to provide extra warmth, with or without a frost blanket.

Industry observers note that colorado State University Extension measured the effect in cold frame trials in Fort Collins. One string of 25 mid-size C7 bulbs hung inside a covered cold frame, with a space blanket over the frame, kept each frame noticeably warmer than the night outside. A string also beat a single large bulb at warming the cold corners.

If you want to recreate an enclosed space like that, use a cold frame or mini greenhouse, but only if the structure allows the lights to be safely suspended away from the plants and covering.

In a recent development, pick up a string of Christmas lights in a store today, and you'll likely find they're LEDs. They convert far more of their electricity into light, leaving little heat behind – fine for decoration but useless for shielding a citrus tree on a 28°F (-2°C) night. When it comes to LED lights, frost protection just isn't on the table – they don't generate enough warmth.

Industry observers note that university frost guidelines specifically recommend incandescent bulbs when you need real heat. Traditional incandescent mini lights can provide some warmth, while larger C7 and C9 bulbs, like these from Novelty Lights Store, produce more heat per bulb.

Any set used should carry an outdoor rating and be suitable for the intended setup. With incandescent Christmas lights, plants under a properly supported cover can gain extra heat, but the same heat makes the bulbs a hazard if they touch foliage or covering materials.

Sources indicate that several vulnerable container plants could benefit, but growers most often protect potted citrus this way. Cold damage can begin around 30°F (-1°C), depending on the variety and duration of exposure, with limes generally more sensitive than mandarins. A potted lemon on the patio faces a specific risk that an in-ground tree doesn't. Its roots are far less cold-hardy than its branches, and the small amount of potting mix around them can cool and freeze much faster than the soil around an in-ground tree.

That means the lights can help through brief cold spells – just a few nights with light frost. They're not enough to protect tropical plants during weeks of hard freezes. A larger container holds more potting mix and can provide some extra insulation for the roots, so a pot like the ModernNest fiberstone planter from Walmart, designed to withstand freezing conditions, gives a citrus tree a sturdier home but won't prevent its roots from freezing.

Recent findings suggest that hot incandescent bulbs can cause damage if they come into contact with foliage or covering materials. Incandescent bulbs can burn leaves if they touch them directly. Frost cloth, sheets, plastic wrap, and space blankets should never be pressed against the lights, where they can scorch, melt, or become a fire risk. Hang the strand so each bulb has enough clearance from surrounding materials, and use a separate frame, stakes, or supports to keep covers up and away from the bulbs. Make sure the lights are securely positioned so they cannot shift into contact with the covering.

Recent findings suggest that water and electricity can create hazards on cold nights. Use only outdoor-rated lights and cords outside, and plug them into a GFCI-protected outlet. Throw out any strand with cracked sockets or frayed wire instead of hanging it. Keep indoor strands and household power strips indoors, and don't rely on tape to waterproof electrical connections. Follow the manufacturer's limits on how many strings can be connected end to end, and follow the safety instructions packed with the product.

Start by moving the pot. An unheated garage, shed, or closed-in porch that stays above freezing can carry a citrus tree through a cold snap with no wiring. Pots that stay outside belong together, up against a house wall or in a corner out of the wind. Water them well before the cold comes, since moist potting mix freezes more slowly than dry.

Covers and wraps add another layer. Lowe's sells a 2-ounce frost blanket that can go over the plant on cold nights and come off during the day. Around the container, slip on an Eonox drawstring pot insulation cover to keep cold wind off the root zone.

For plants that need steady heat for weeks, a thermostatically controlled heater inside a greenhouse built to house one is the safer setup – the Dr Infrared greenhouse heater has an adjustable thermostat.

Under a cover or in a cold frame, old incandescent holiday lights can add a few degrees, maybe enough to see potted citrus through a short, light frost. You can't count on them, though, and the method needs careful setup, even though it's recommended by several university extension services. An LED strand won't give a cold plant any real protection.

Sources indicate that using hot bulbs with fabric and outdoor power for improvised heating carries risks that are easy to underestimate. Proper shelter, insulation, and a good frost blanket are generally safer options, although they won't always provide as much warmth as a safely heated enclosure.

For most gardeners, the simplest solution is to keep the twinkling lights on the porch this year and move your lemon tree into a frost-free garage when cold weather hits. It'll still be green when the holiday decorations go back in the attic.

Christmas Cactus Not Blooming? 5 Common Mistakes That Stop the Holiday Flower Show

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1243 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Christmas cactus not blooming is a common holiday letdown, and it stings more when the plant seems perfectly healthy with plump green stems.
  • A healthy Christmas cactus doesn't automatically mean you have a holiday houseplant that's ready to flower.
  • There are five common mistakes that lead to zero holiday flowers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Christmas cactus not blooming is a common holiday letdown, and it stings more when the plant seems perfectly healthy with plump green stems. And you ask yourself, why won't my Christmas cactus flower when the plant looks just fine? A Christmas cactus not showing buds by the end of November is usually reacting to light, warmth, water or a move at the wrong moment. And, once you've worked out what the cause is, there's still time to fix some mistakes so you can enjoy the holiday flower show.

A healthy Christmas cactus doesn't automatically mean you have a holiday houseplant that's ready to flower. Buds form in response to fall conditions – long dark nights and cooler temperatures – and many folk create the exact environment to make sure a Christmas cactus blooms right on time for the holidays. So, unless it gets those triggers to start forming buds, the plant won't flower even if you give your Christmas cactus all the care it needs in November to keep it healthy. Another common problem with a Christmas cactus not flowering is that it does form buds, but drops them before they open.

There are five common mistakes that lead to zero holiday flowers. Which of these problems is the reason why your Christmas cactus doesn't have buds yet?

Sources indicate that holiday cacti set flower buds when nights grow long. They need about 13 to 14 hours of uninterrupted darkness each night for six weeks or more, and that dark period must be truly dark. Even a table lamp switched on in the evening, a street light shining through the window or a hallway light left on overnight can interrupt the cycle, causing the plant to keep making stems instead of buds. This mistake reveals up as no buds at all.

In a recent development, if you suspect this is the reason your Schlumbergera doesn't have buds yet, place your plant in complete darkness after dinner then bring it back to bright, indirect light in the morning. A dark room that isn't used is perfect, and you can block any artificial light coming through the window with blackout curtains like Sun Zero Curtain Panels, available from Walmart. Another option is simply to cover the plant in an upturned cardboard box overnight.

Once buds have set, night length stops mattering as much, so evening light isn't a problem.

Cool nights are the other half of the trigger to get a Christmas cactus to flower. Holiday cacti need nights between 50°F and 59°F (10–15°C) to set buds, so keep a living room warm all evening with the furnace running and that signal disappears.

According to recent reports, move your Christmas cactus to a cooler spot at night, not a cold one. An unheated bedroom or a sunroom that cools down after dark often works, as long as temperature doesn't dip below 50°F (10°C). It's hard to guess how cool a room gets at three o'clock in the morning so a cheap indoor thermometer that records the maximum and minimum temperatures, like the TempPro digital indoor thermometer on Amazon, is handy to check the overnight number.

Once your plant has formed buds, it'' still very sensitive to environmental conditions, so be sure to avoid the common spots that cause a Christmas cactus to lose its buds.

Holiday cacti aren't desert cacti. They grow on rainforest trees in Brazil so don't like to bake dry the way a barrel cactus loves. Let the potting mix dry out hard while buds are forming and the plant may make fewer of them, or wilt and drop the ones it has. Keep the mix soggy and the roots can rot, which ends the same way – limp stems and buds on the floor.

Once buds appear, keep the potting mix evenly moist but never wet. An easy way to check if your Christmas cactus needs watering is to push a long wooden skewer like these bamboo skewers from Walmart to the bottom of the pot and pull it out: if damp soil clings to the wood, wait a few days before watering again. An indoor watering can with a long goose-neck spout like this houseplant can from Walmart makes it much easier to be precise about how much water you're giving your plant. Empty the saucer after every watering too.

Once buds have formed, moving your plant is one of the easiest ways to lose them. Any sudden shift in light, temperature or humidity can trigger bud loss. Christmas cacti are so sensitive to their environment, it's not just moving the plant from a cool back bedroom to a warm, dim spot beside the tree that causes bud drop. Even moving your holiday houseplant to a different spot in the same room or rotating the pot can be enough to lose those precious buds.

Choose the spot where your plant will stay through the holidays as soon as buds appear, then leave it there. Check that spot for heat and drafts first. Buds also drop on plants near heating vents, a gas fireplace or a bowl of ripening fruit which gives off ethylene gas. The same care applies if you buy a plant with buds already set, such as this pack of 2 Holiday Christmas Cactus from Costa Farms, via The Home Depot. Ask for the plant to be wrapped against the cold for the trip home and put it in its final spot as soon as it arrives. A few buds will fall while it settles in but most will stay put as long as you don't move the plant again.

Holiday cacti should only be fed during active growth from spring through late summer, so don't fertilize after September. That break from fertilizer helps plants set more flower buds in fall. November feeding won't help a plant that already lacks buds and, on a stressed plant, extra salts in the pot do more harm than good.

Recent findings suggest that wait until the flowers finish and upcoming growth starts in spring, then use a balanced food for indoor flowering plants such as Espoma Organic Violet! plant food, available on Amazon, once a month at half strength through summer.

If you don't see any signs of buds on your holiday houseplant by late November, it's worth trying the banana bag trick to trigger Christmas cactus blooms. However, flowers will likely open in early January rather than on Christmas morning.

Next year, start the dark nights in late September or early October so the timing lines up. Buds usually show up three to four weeks after long nights begin, and the flowers open after roughly six to eight weeks of short days.

A plant that already has small buds at its stem tips in mid-November has done the hard part, however, so as long as you keep your Christmas cactus in one spot that's not too warm at night, and evenly moist, those flowers should open on schedule.

Miller filed the suit after the Daily Mail published a story reporting that Miller "hurled a pot of boiling water" at Moreno during an argument, and later wrote a note apologizing for the incident. As the court notes, an audio recording (that Miller released somehow thinking it would exonerate him) confirms the core of the claim. From the opinion:.

Plaintiff maintains that the gist or sting of hurling a pot of boiling water is "categorically different" than the actions Plaintiff states actually occurred. It is Plaintiffs burden to support his claims with credible, admissible evidence. Plaintiff has not shown that the statement about dousing Defendant Moreno with boiling hot water are false. The imputation that Plaintiff poured or doused Defendant Moreno with hot water is substantially true.

The court also noted the lack of any evidence that Moreno was responsible for the Daily Mail's publication of the claims.

Turn a Cheap Christmas Tree Into a Showstopper – 6 Easy Steps to Make It Lush and Luxurious

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1370 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that when you take the kids out to choose a Christmas tree, everyone has in mind a lush, deep green, perfectly shaped evergreen that is featured in holiday advertisements.
  • But don’t worry, an inexpensive grocery store Christmas tree can be “spruced up” nicely with a few simple tricks.
  • In this guide, I'm going to walk you through the easy steps you can take to improve your tree dramatically, from a sparse Christmas tree to a festive showstopper.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when you take the kids out to choose a Christmas tree, everyone has in mind a lush, deep green, perfectly shaped evergreen that is featured in holiday advertisements. But not every evergreen in the lot has that kind of sex appeal, especially budget trees for sale in grocery stores, supermarkets, and big-box retailers. These affordable trees can look thin, sparse, and like they didn’t get any sleep last night.

But don’t worry, an inexpensive grocery store Christmas tree can be “spruced up” nicely with a few simple tricks. Yes, you can turn ugly ducklings into beautiful centerpieces by taking steps to make a Christmas tree look fuller, well-structured, and fresh. I’ll explain how to make a real Christmas tree look better with Christmas tree care tips that boost your tree's wow-power.

In this guide, I'm going to walk you through the easy steps you can take to improve your tree dramatically, from a sparse Christmas tree to a festive showstopper. And I promise it won’t cost you a fortune.

There are many reasons that a freshly cut Christmas tree can look droopy and sparse in the store. These include transport stress and dehydration. One of the quickest fixes with a massive punch is to make a fresh cut on the bottom of the trunk, taking off around ½ inch. A good folding saw, such as the Rexberi 11-Inch Folding Saw from Amazon, will make light work of this, and it's handy for pruning jobs around the garden, too.

According to recent reports, immediately after cutting, pop the tree into a sturdy stand with water. The Krinner Genie Christmas Tree Stand has a foot-pedal mechanism that makes it easy to secure the tree, plus a built-in water reservoir. But it's not cheap, and if you're buying a budget tree, chances are you'll want a budget-friendly stand to go with it. The Leejec Christmas Tree Stand is a good, affordable alternative, with a generous water reservoir and a handy water level indicator.

Don't leave the tree sitting around after making the cut. The cut surface can dry out, reducing moisture uptake, so getting it into water promptly gives it the best chance of staying fresh.

That sorrowful evergreen you brought home needs time to relax. Once you prune off the very bottom of the trunk, set the tree in a bucket of water and give it time to rehydrate. Leave it wrapped in its netting overnight, which will also make it easier to maneuver into its stand the next day.

Sources indicate that once the tree is securely in place, remove the wrapping and let the branches gradually drop and spread into their natural shape for a few hours. You might be surprised how much fuller it looks after a little time to settle.

Sources indicate that now it's time to give your tree a little makeover. Walk around it and look carefully at its shape. There will likely be a few stray or uneven branches that need tidying up, particularly if you've bought a cheaper tree that hasn't been professionally shaped.

It has been revealed that to prune your Christmas tree, take a sharp pair of bypass pruners – Fiskars Bypass Pruning Shears from Amazon are a good, affordable option – and start by removing any broken, damaged, or awkwardly protruding branches. Trim back overly long branches to a side shoot where possible, rather than cutting bluntly through the tips.

In a recent development, pay particular attention to the lower branches. Remove any that drag on the floor or interfere with the stand, making clean cuts close to the trunk without damaging the bark. This will give the tree a neater silhouette and make it easier to reach the water reservoir.

Step back regularly to check your progress, working toward a balanced cone shape without making the tree look unnaturally perfect. Go easy, though – you can always take more off, but you can't put a branch back.

Starting at the bottom of the tree, gently separate any branches that have become compressed during transport. Work your way upward, easing crowded branches apart and encouraging them to spread into their natural positions. Take care not to force stiff branches, as they can snap.

In a recent development, once you've worked your way around the tree, step back and look for any obvious gaps. You may be able to gently reposition flexible branches to make the tree look fuller, but avoid bending or twisting them into unnatural shapes.

Pay particular attention to the lower branches, spreading them outward where possible to help disguise the trunk and tree stand. Near the top, gently separate crowded branches to create a more balanced, tapered shape. Don't worry about making everything perfectly symmetrical – a little natural irregularity is part of the charm of a real Christmas tree.

Have you ever used hair extensions? Or had a friend who used hair weaving to change the volume of their hair? You can use this same technique to fill in the canopy of your Christmas tree by tucking extra evergreen branches into bare spots. It’s a quick way to give a sparse Christmas tree a fuller figure.

In a recent development, what to use for this type of branch extension? Start with any healthy branches you removed when pruning your tree earlier. You can also use evergreen clippings from your own yard or ask for spare branches from the Christmas tree lot. Choose branches that closely match your tree for the most natural finish, or mix two or three types of evergreen to add depth and texture.

Recent findings suggest that for larger bare patches, try tucking in realistic faux evergreen sprays, like these Hananona pine branches. Cedar and pine sprays work particularly well, blending into the natural foliage while adding extra volume.

Recent findings suggest that tuck the cut ends in toward the trunk, positioning the foliage to disguise any obvious gaps. Use green floral wire, like this Pauleen wire from Amazon, to secure the stems discreetly to existing branches, making sure they're firmly attached. Step back occasionally to check the overall effect, adding a few more sprigs wherever the tree still looks sparse.

We all have good sides and bad sides, and your Christmas tree might too. If one side is lopsided or less impressive, simply turn it toward the wall. Of course, this trick works less well if you have a revolving tree stand.

Some gaps may still be visible after fluffing up the branches and adding extras, but that's where clever decorating comes to the rescue. Tuck large ornaments deep inside the tree, closer to the trunk, to disguise bare spots and create a sense of depth.

It has been revealed that another great trick is to cluster smaller ornaments in groups of three to make sparse areas look fuller. If one part of the tree is overloaded with decorations, move a few into the gaps to create a more balanced look. You can also use pinecones, artificial flowers, or decorative picks to add texture and interest.

It has been revealed that finally, try weaving wide ribbons or garlands through the branches to disguise any remaining gaps. Rather than wrapping them tightly around the outside, tuck sections deeper into the tree and let them billow outward. This creates the illusion of a much fuller, more luxurious Christmas tree without spending a fortune.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some excerpts from the longish decision Friday by Judge Benjamin Beaton (E.D. Ky.) in Woodcock v. Capilouto:.

This opinion addresses the latest chapter in the ongoing saga concerning Professor Ramsi Woodcock, his commentary regarding Israel and Palestine, and the University of Kentucky's investigation into whether he violated Title VI or the school's technology or conduct policies….

Earlier this month, this Court denied law professor Ramsi Woodcock's request to halt the University of Kentucky's ongoing investigation into several comments he made related to his views on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and his 2025 "Petition for Military Action Against Israel." Woodcock's initial submissions had not persuasively shown that the investigation was retaliatory in its origin or chilling in its ongoing effect.

But the order set an evidentiary hearing two weeks later to address these fact-dependent questions and Woodcock's request for a preliminary injunction. The investigation—which had lasted more than a year and whose report was already overdue—could not "last forever" without threatening Woodcock's First Amendment rights. And the University of Kentucky's corresponding "reassignment" of Woodcock from teaching duties throughout the investigation was increasingly hard to justify, particularly given the absence of any articulated suspicion of classroom disruption….

Then, one week after the TRO decision, the outside investigator's 134-page sealed (for now) report finally landed. {That report is provisionally under seal pending the resolution of a motion to seal, which will be referred to a Magistrate Judge.} ….

[Now], the Dean of the law school could decide whether to lift Woodcock's reassignment from teaching and restore him to the classroom for the spring semester. This could happen as late as mid-December, according to counsel, without prejudicing Woodcock's ability to teach…. [And] the University President could decide, based on the investigative report, whether (in his view) Woodcock violated any laws or policies….

The report and Woodcock's response have been published by the Kentucky Lantern (McKenna Horsley); Woodcock reports that this is because they were publicly filed in a parallel state case. The court had this to say about Woodcock's request for a temporary injunction to block any findings by the University President:.

Sources indicate that during previous hearings, this Court observed that Woodcock's effort to end his reassignment from teaching stood on firmer ground that his request to halt the investigation itself. That view rested largely on caselaw that contemplated speech-related investigations consistent with the First Amendment yet considered whether any attendant consequences of such investigations abridged those rights based on a retaliatory purpose, chilled speech, or both. {See generally, e.g., Sensabaugh v. Halliburton (6th Cir. 2019) (no adverse action based on "letter of guidance" and reprimand in the context of a "independent law firm" investigation involving "scores of documents and text messages" and "seventeen different witnesses"); Moore v. Garnand (9th Cir. 2023) ("[W]e never held that a retaliatory investigation alone could violate the First Amendment, as our holding rested on much more than just a retaliatory investigation[.]").} ….

Woodcock insists that the First Amendment bars the President from spending "weeks poring over documents" unrelated to "any arguable policy violation." "Whatever the University decides about spring teaching, findings issued on the investigator's report would injure Woodcock irreparably on their own." To the extent that review entails an inquiry into his political beliefs, Woodcock contends, the process is illegitimate and should be enjoined immediately….

[But] a substantial body of caselaw indicates that a speech-related investigation alone generally doesn't amount to retaliation or adverse action. {See, e.g., Churchill v. Univ. of Colorado at Boulder (Colo. App. 2010) ("Courts have concluded that investigations alone are not adverse employment actions."); Sensabaugh (6th Cir. 2019) (concluding no adverse action even when context included a "painstakin[g] investigation"); Couch v. Board. of Trustees of Memorial Hospital of Carbon County (10th Cir. 2009) (investigation didn't amount to adverse action supporting First Amendment retaliation); Benningfield v. City of Houston (5th Cir. 1998) ("Although a reprimand can constitute an adverse employment action, an investigation does not[.]"); Moore ("[W]e have never held that a retaliatory investigation alone could violate the First Amendment"); Bell v. Sheriff of Broward County 1375 (11th Cir. 2021) ("[D]eputy Bell's five-day suspension with pay pending an investigation into his conduct is not an adverse action."). But as emphasized in the Court's previous TRO opinion, the caselaw in this area is hardly uniform and uncertainty remains about how different circuits might approach each specific factual scenario. See, e.g., Holt v. Pennsylvania (3d Cir. 2017) ("Our Circuit has not considered whether the initiation of an internal investigation can constitute an 'adverse action' for purposes of a First Amendment retaliation claim, and our sister circuits are split on the glitch.").} The collateral consequences of an investigation, by contrast, may create an intolerable chill that could warrant judicial intervention. See, e.g., Levin v. Harleston (2d Cir. 1992); White v. Lee (9th Cir. 2000). The First Amendment leaves at least some room for employers to investigate their employees for perceived misconduct, even when the alleged offenses relate to speech. Waters v. Churchill (1994) (plurality op.) ("Only [investigative] procedures outside the range" of reasonableness violate First Amendment despite investigation's "risk of erroneously punishing protected speech."); Gartenberg v. Cooper Union (S.D.N.Y. 2025) (even protected speech may be relevant to determining "whether actionable harassment occurred").

It has been revealed that woodcock hasn't pointed to any precedent halting a school's investigation based only on its existence or the "brand" or "reputational harm" that it might produce. To the contrary, the two precedents on which he relies most heavily are easily distinguishable.

Sources indicate that sweezy v. Newly introduced Hampshire (1957), is a 70-year-old precedent concerning a state attorney general's investigation into a professor's affiliation with the Communist and Progressive Parties. It had little, if anything, to say about the operations, autonomy, or academic interests of a university. Contra, e.g., Regents of University of Michigan v. Ewing (1985).

Fischer v. Thomas (6th Cir. 2022), likewise sits far afield from the context of university governance and academic speech. In that pre-enforcement challenge, the Sixth Circuit barred a state judicial commission from initiating formal proceedings against two judicial candidates after it "sen[t] vague and threatening letter to [the] candidates on the eve of election." The opinion didn't address whether an investigation or its concluding findings amounted to adverse action or retaliation….

Fifth, even assuming Woodcock could establish a likelihood of success on the merits of his retaliation claim, to obtain a TRO he'd have to show irreparable harm and the balance of the equities relative to third parties and the public. Irreparable harm likely requires at least some showing of subjective chill as well; otherwise a court would be left to wonder why and "whether it needs to act now." ….

The current record does precious little to "identify speech that [Woodcock] wishes to make in the future but for the threat of prosecution of that future speech." Despite boilerplate assertions that he'd otherwise say and write more about Israel and Palestine, it's hardly clear that this investigation has chilled Woodcock's speech at all. He points to a paper called "A Law and Economics Argument for Ending Israel" that he hasn't yet submitted to the law reviews; diminished posting on his blog, called "the Antizionist Legal Studies Movement;" and allegedly decreased Twitter activity. Yet Woodcock's social-media and listserv posting hasn't stopped altogether; during this investigation he has continued to post on X and the AALS online discussion groups, including about Israel; he has filed at least four lawsuits, several of which have been covered in the press; he maintains a webpage supplying information about and soliciting support for his speech and litigation. Without further evidence, the Court cannot conclude that Woodcock will be chilled over the next two weeks.

Although the general tendency in the caselaw to treat First Amendment violations as irreparable harm cautions against assigning dispositive weight to this factor, the weakness of Woodcock's showing on the current record at least cuts against automatic or presumptive injunctive relief to ameliorate any purported self-censorship….

The court also pointed to the university's own interest in speaking about Woodcock's speech:.

It has been revealed that [A]n injunction barring the President from reacting to the investigator's findings would—even on Woodcock's own terms—remedy one arguable free-speech violation with another. As any law professor knows, Justice Brandeis taught that the "remedy" for disfavored speech should ordinarily be more speech—not additional suppression. A college president, just like a law professor, may presumptively speak—privately or publicly—about a matter of public and professional interest such as this. Indeed, both have done so during this process.

Industry observers note that and President Capiluto's own speech rights aren't the only countervailing interests at matter. The University has its own governance interests in the orderly and prompt resolution of a high-profile pending investigation. See Ewing ("Academic freedom thrives not only on the independent and uninhibited exchange of ideas among teachers and students, … but also, and somewhat inconsistently, on autonomous decisionmaking by the academy itself."). "Without this ability to investigate, a public employer would be left without recourse and would lose its 'greater leeway in its dealings with citizen employees.'".

Given these compounding considerations, the Court concluded that no temporary order revisiting the Court's prior orders and specifically restraining the President was warranted based on these allegations of objective chill (regarding Woodcock's likelihood of success on the merits), subjective chill (regarding any irreparable harm associated with Woodcock's speech pending the forthcoming presidential findings), or the public and third-party interest in an orderly and prompt conclusion to an academic investigation….

In a recent development, this order, to be clear, does not resolve whether the University officials' past actions constituted retaliation in violation of the First Amendment—a distinct and retrospective question, for which damages and attorney fees under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1983 & 1988 are at least potentially available (though the Defendants of course disagree). While those historical facts are necessary to Woodcock's showing of likelihood of success on the merits, even if proved they are not sufficient to warrant a restraining order, which requires a showing of ongoing chilled speech.

Nor does this order address the propriety of any discipline that Woodcock might eventually face. As described above, those questions haven't ripened and follow their own administrative process—one the Sixth Circuit specifically contemplated might alter the abstention analysis….

Traditions connect generations, carrying the cultural and moral values of ancestors to upcoming generations, giving them a sense of identity and belonging. Some of these traditions are so lovely that they are adopted more widely. The beautiful old Christmas tradition of Christmas wheat is one of them.

The sowing of Christmas wheat is a tradition across Europe from France to Ukraine and the Balkans. Early in December, people “plant” wheatgrass seeds in bowls indoors early in December and let the shoots grow until Christmas. Initially the growing wheat seeds were considered a blessing for the coming harvest. But beyond that, the green shoots have come to symbolize fertility, newly introduced life, and eternal renewal.

It has been revealed that you don’t have to live in the South of France or other parts of Europe to practice this lovely tradition. We’ll tell you all about the custom of growing wheatgrass indoors and how you can make it your own this Christmas.

All around the globe, cultural heritage shapes how people celebrate, and also how they express beauty. The lovely tradition of planting Christmas wheat is still very much a part of Christmas festivities in Europe, thought to have been inherited from the Romans.

Industry observers note that it is practiced in the Province area of France, as well as Croatia, Ukraine, and parts of Italy and Portugal, each region claiming it as their own. In Province, it is called Saint-Barbe wheat (le blé de la Sainte-Barbe) because the day of planting, December 4, is the feast day of Saint Barbara. By Christmas day, the seeds have grown fresh green shoots that become decorations on the Christmas table.

Industry observers note that in Province, this age-old tradition involves sprouting grains of wheat in three separate bowls. The ritual is said to ensure prosperity and happiness for the coming year, a promise memorialized in the old Provençal adage, “when wheat goes well, everything goes well.”.

According to recent reports, in Croatia, the origins of this tradition are still related to religion, but they are different. Growing wheatgrass is related to the story of the holy family fleeing Herod’s soldiers. It is remarked that the family found a farmer sowing wheat. The family requested that the farmer tell the Herod’s soldiers that the family had already passed through.

Recent findings suggest that the wheat grew remarkably fast that year so by the time the soldiers came, there was a fine crop. Then, the farmer told them that the family passed through while he was sowing his crop. Because the wheat was so tall, the soldiers assumed that the family had passed by long ago and abandoned their quest. As such, wheat seeds are sown in December to represent light found amid the winter's darkness.

So, how to grow your own wheat?

Well, if you would like to incorporate this ancient tradition into your own holiday celebrations, we’ll walk you through the steps. There are three: gather what you need, “plant” the seeds, then arrange the centerpiece.

Recent findings suggest that the most notable "ingredient" you will require to grow your own Christmas wheat are the wheat grains themselves. Traditionally, you use hard red winter wheat berries (sold as "wheatgrass seeds”) although it is possible to use alternatives like lentils or chickpeas instead.

Recent findings suggest that the presentation also varies from region to region. In Province, for Saint Barbe’s wheat, they use three small bowls or saucers and damp cotton wool. The three containers have religious significance, representing the Holy Trinity. In Croatia, you can use any container, but you still need to line it with either cotton wool or soil as a growing medium. A more practical alternative is to use a growing tray filled with potting soil with a solid tray beneath it to catch water.

It has been revealed that soak the grains overnight in water. After that, place them evenly on the growing medium - like the bed of damp cotton wool or the potting soil. If you are using three bowls, spread it evenly between them. If you are using a tray, spread the seeds there.

Place the seeded container near a bright window at a mild temperature. Spray it with water and cover with plastic paper or a plastic bag. Remove this plastic when the seeds begin to germinate.

In a recent development, mist the cotton with water daily to keep it moist. This allows the shoots to germinate and grow straight and green.

How you choose to arrange the centerpiece depends entirely on your own preferences and traditions. By Christmas Eve, the little shoots are green and straight,.

In Croatia, the wheat sprouts are often decorated with the Croatian tricolour – a red-white-blue ribbon. This adds patriotic symbolism. The Croatians sometimes add a red candle or even a red apple in the centre of the container to add more holiday cheer.

According to recent reports, in Province, the French often toe up the sprouted wheat with red and yellow or red and green ribbons. The wheat display becomes the centerpiece for their traditional Christmas Eve feast. After Christmas, the French place the pots in or near the family crèche (aka the nativity scene) alongside handmade clay saint images. Finally, the wheat can be planted in open ground or burned in the fireplace for protection.

In a recent development, remember, this is a lovely tradition, but while wheatgrass might look like a microgreen it should not be used as one. Yes, it has many incredible health properties (it is said to prevent some types of cancer, fight infection and improve cognitive function), but it is not edible.

It has been revealed that that being mentioned, you can juice it and drink its juice, which is full of vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants. Sounds like a great tipple after a major holiday feast, eh?

💡 Key Takeaways

  • That recipe is Marvel Meal, and if you're feeding birds on a budget, it's hard to beat.
  • Chickadees, titmice, and wrens come for the soft dough – and so do bluebirds, which don't always bother with a seed feeder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Go down the bird food aisle this time of year and the choices just keep going, from seed blends to suet cakes in a dozen flavors. Some people walk right past all of it. They make their own at home, and one old recipe shows up in their kitchens again and again.

That recipe is Marvel Meal, and if you're feeding birds on a budget, it's hard to beat. The whole batch is peanut butter, vegetable shortening, cornmeal, and flour. Odds are you've got all four in the cupboard right now.

Chickadees, titmice, and wrens come for the soft dough – and so do bluebirds, which don't always bother with a seed feeder. It's cheap, it keeps in the freezer, and kids can help mix it. And if you love helping birds in your backyard, then enter our competition to win a Birdfy smart feeder.

Sources indicate that its exact origin is hard to pin down, but bluebird fans have been passing the recipe around for years, and Penn State Extension still shares it today. There's nothing to cook and no beef fat to render, which some suet recipes call for. You also won't find a ring of spilled seed under the feeder the way you do with a seed mix.

Insect eaters get the most out of it. Bluebirds rarely eat seeds, and woodpeckers, nuthatches, and wrens lean on insects for much of the year. Come winter, bugs get hard to find. A rich, fatty food fills that gap with the calories birds need to stay warm through long nights, at a time when natural food can be scarce.

Beat the peanut butter and shortening together in a substantial bowl until it's smooth. Then work in the cornmeal and flour a cup or so at a time, and stir the seeds in last. You're after a soft dough that holds its shape when you squeeze a lump of it. If kids are helping, check for peanut allergies before anyone digs in.

Marvel Meal doesn't need to go in the fridge first. Soft is good, since that's what lets you press it into a feeder. If you'd rather have firm blocks for a suet feeder, spread the dough in a pan lined with wax paper, freeze it, and cut it into pieces.

According to recent reports, log feeders, like this Pennington red cedar suet feeder from Walmart, are the old standby. Press the dough into the drilled holes. You can also just smear some on rough bark or a pinecone, or fill half a coconut shell.

Sources indicate that place frozen blocks of Marvel Meal in a basic suet cage, like this Kingsyard all-metal double suet bird feeder with perch. The cage keeps squirrels and bigger birds from making off with the whole chunk. But never use a mesh onion bag – birds can get their feet tangled and stuck.

For bluebirds, roll the dough into small balls and set them in an open dish with some cover over it. Audubon's Woodlink dome-top seed and bluebird feeder, available at Home Depot, has a roof right above the dish. Wet weather turns the dough to mush, and a clear plastic squirrel baffle hung over a hanging feeder helps keep the rain off. Don't put out more than the birds will clean up in a day or two.

Industry observers note that penn State lists chickadees, titmice, wrens, and bluebirds as fans. Woodpeckers, nuthatches, blue jays, and even cardinals stop by too, though European starlings can turn into pests.

According to recent reports, bluebirds are the hard ones. They don't go to feeders the way chickadees do, and a lot of them have to learn that a dish means food. Who demonstrates up in your yard depends on what lives around you and how you set out the food. Try a couple of spots and give it a few days. Hang feeders near trees or shrubs so small birds have somewhere to dart, just not so close that a hawk can sit hidden in them.

Marvel Meal is a winter treat, not a year-round meal. Start putting it out when the nights get cold in late fall and natural food is getting scarce. Birds don't need a steady diet of rich food, and heat brings its own problems. When highs climb to about 65°F to 70°F (18–21°C), the fat goes soft and can go rancid – and greasy food can mat feathers and even get onto eggs in a nest. Once spring stays warm, take it down.

Leftover dough keeps in sealed bags in the fridge, and the extra can go in the freezer. Keep seed somewhere cool and dry as well. The Gamma2 Vittles Vault from Walmart holds up to 35 pounds (16kg). Toss anything that's moldy, wet, or smells rancid. About every two weeks, scrub feeders in a mix of 1 part bleach to 9 parts water, and do it more often when it's wet or the feeders are busy. Rinse them well and let them dry before you fill them again.

Fill a log with Marvel Meal on a frosty morning, and a chickadee will probably find it before your coffee gets cold. Keep the batches small and the feeders clean, and they'll stick around all winter.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2020, during the early days of the pandemic, the House of Representatives adopted a rule that would allow absent members to cast a vote by proxy. At the time, there were ample warnings that this process had constitutional infirmities, but the House pressed ahead. Indeed, the House of Representatives continued to use the proxy rule through the end of 2022. One such bill was the Consolidation Appropriations Act of 2023. At this time, the justification for social distancing had passed. The upcoming House assembled in January 2023. I see no masks. Members of Congress are walking around with their families.

At the 2023 State of the Union Address in March 2023, every every seat was filled. Look at this picture. I don't see many members wearing masks.

Don't tell me there was some actual need to bypass the quorum rule at this point.

Sources indicate that the pandemic was only a few years ago, but it is key to remember how many brazen violations of the Constitution there were in short order. As Justice Gorsuch wrote in Roman Catholic Diocese v. Brooklyn v. Cuomo, "Even if the Constitution has taken a holiday during this pandemic, it cannot become a sabbatical." The proxy rule was one such sabbatical.

In 2023, Texas challenged the constitutionality of one provision of the appropriations bill, the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act. In 2024, Judge Hendrix of the Northern District of Texas wrote a magisterial opinion that stretched more than one-hundred pages. He explained in depth why the enrolled bill doctrine does not block review and why the proxy rule violates the quorum clause. At the time, I read the opinion and thought Judge Hendrix put forward an extremely justification. The House tried to take a shortcut and got caught. A panel of the Fifth Circuit reversed, but now the en banc Fifth Circuit has affirmed Judge Hendrix's decision.

I'll admit, the immediate reaction to this decision is "it can't be right!" This intuition, I submit, is based more on the consequences than the merits. If every bill passed during the COVID period is now subject to a constitutional challenge, the consequences could be serious. But I encourage you to back off the consequentialism. Far too many judges and lawyers start with the consequences and work their way backwards. If the House of Representatives decided to take a shortcut and ignored a constitutional requirement, then the members of that body should bear the consequences of their decision.

According to recent reports, the en banc Fifth Circuit split (as if often does) by a 9-8 vote. Thankfully, there were no senior judges on the three-judge panel. Judge Wilson wrote the majority opinion and Judge Graves wrote the dissent. Judge Haynes continues her unusual practice where she doesn't join any opinion, reducing her thoughts to a single footnote.

According to recent reports, * Judge Haynes states that she does not think it is appropriate to throw out the Federal House of Representatives in this arena, so she dissents. She also appreciates Judge Graves's dissent.

Recent findings suggest that judge Haynes might think she is being clever, but I doubt anyone else agrees. Indeed, in a number of recent cases, Judge Haynes simply writes that she affirms for the reasons stated by the district court--as if nothing that her colleagues wrote made a difference. I think it shows a lack of respect to her colleagues who spend considerable time preparing opinions and she doesn't even bother explaining where she disagrees. She is capable of writing reasoned opinions, but just shrugs at the en banc stage.

Recent findings suggest that judges Wilson and Judge Graves agree that Texas has standing. They further agree that the enrolled bill rule does not preclude review. The disagreement is purely a legal question about whether the proxy rule violates the Quorum Clause. Having read both the majority and dissenting opinions, I don't think the glitch is even close. The strongest argument for the dissent is the "Unanimous Consent" rule, and the majority demolishes that argument.

Sources indicate that what happens next? It's complicated.

I am fairly certain that the new Attorney General opposes this case and will do everything in his power to scuttle the suit, as well as the Fifth Circuit's en banc precedent. In recent days, the Texas Attorney General has been dismissing and settling many cases. The reason, I suspect, is to avoid giving the new Attorney General a vehicle to enter into binding consent decrees. I suppose it is conceivable that Texas will try to enter into some kind of settlement with the United States. Or maybe Texas just moves to dismiss the case with prejudice before January 1. That would end the case, but leave the Fifth Circuit's precedent in place.

I suppose another state with a similar Article III injury could intervene. I am not certain about the timing as there is a final judgment in place--although a judgment is not really final until a cert petition is disposed of.

If this case stays alive past January, the United States will almost certainly file a cert petition. The new Texas Attorney General will not oppose certiorari and may ask for a summary reversal. I suspect the new AG could even argue that since there is no adversity, there is no longer a live Article III case, and the Fifth Circuit decision should be vacated under Musingwear. I am not entirely sure how Munsingwear applies when the Attorney General switches sides, but we may soon find out. Then again, the Supreme Court routinely decides cases in which there is no adversity, so the case might continue.

In a recent development, indeed, the Supreme Court might also think it prudent to settle this matter. These challenges can arise in other contexts, and the longer this issue festers, the worse it will be. If so, the Court could appoint an amicus to defend the Fifth Circuit's judgment.

At that point, what will happen? Again, all members of the Fifth Circuit agreed that Texas has standing and the enrolled bill rule doesn't bar review. I suppose the Supreme Court could reject those holdings, but that would be rather transparent.

Sources indicate that once you get to the merits, the Court will have to do some work. I've seen some commentators lead of with a discussion of how many laws might be at risk. One of those statutes is the Electoral Count Reform Act of 2022. I'll close where I started. The meaning of the Constitution should not change based on the consequences. Either the House had a quorum or it didn't.

Do I have faith that a majority of the Supreme Court will follow that original meaning of the Constitution? No, I don't. Maybe three votes, at the most--which is often how the Fifth Circuit fares. But don't pretend the Supreme Court is making its ruling based on law.

#113232. Eco-Friendly Hardscaping Ideas for a More Sustainable Garden

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1005 w)

Eco-Friendly Hardscaping Ideas for a More Sustainable Garden

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1005 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finegardening

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The increasingly common term “eco-friendly” encourages us to think more carefully about the products and practices we use every day.
  • According to recent reports, it’s exciting to have such a vast and diverse selection of landscape materials available for our designs and garden improvements, but many of those options have a significant impact on our planet through their creation, shipping, and installation.
  • With 30 years of experience as a landscape designer, I’ve recommended countless decks, patios, paths, fences, and other hardscaping elements to my clients, admittedly with minimal guidance about the actual materials used.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The increasingly common term “eco-friendly” encourages us to think more carefully about the products and practices we use every day. When applied to hardscaping, it brings to mind materials and techniques that minimize environmental impacts and reduce our carbon footprints.

According to recent reports, it’s exciting to have such a vast and diverse selection of landscape materials available for our designs and garden improvements, but many of those options have a significant impact on our planet through their creation, shipping, and installation. By thinking about how our hardscaping choices affect natural resources, pollution, and local ecosystems, we can create landscapes that are attractive, functional, and potentially more affordable.

With 30 years of experience as a landscape designer, I’ve recommended countless decks, patios, paths, fences, and other hardscaping elements to my clients, admittedly with minimal guidance about the actual materials used. In recent years, I’ve seen a notable uptick in clients who have expressed strong interest in locally sourced materials and in repurposing or recycling materials for these features.

Some have even accumulated reclaimed bricks, large concrete pieces, and other materials with the intent of incorporating them into the design. This is exciting to me, as designs should balance the durability and longevity of products with a focus on resource efficiency and environmentally friendly options. These creative approaches are becoming more readily available and are being sought out by eco-savvy gardeners.

Read More: How Space and Structure Create a Living Oasis.

It has been revealed that conventional hardscape materials have a “production history” that often comes with a heavy environmental cost. This might include the lumber we purchase, edging materials, or the pavers and path materials we specify. Their history includes not only energy and resources used in production but also shipping and transport, and ultimately, their disposal or reuse at the end of their useful lives.

Finding lower-impact materials takes some research, but sustainability doesn’t have to come at the expense of durability or functionality. Interestingly, eco-friendly options can be more cost-effective over the long run because of lower maintenance needs and durability.

Hardscaping elements such as decks and fences are great examples to explore. Decades ago, the question for clients in my Midwest location was “cedar or treated pine” for most fences or decks. Now, the evolution and wider availability of composite decking and recycled plastic lumber have created increasingly popular alternatives.

Industry observers note that of course, the manufacture of composite lumber isn’t carbon neutral, and its environmental benefits depend on the materials and manufacturing processes involved. However, products incorporating recycled materials can reduce demand for virgin resources, and their durability may offer advantages over time.

Another option for traditional wood features is to seek out responsibly sourced, third-party-certified lumber, such as wood carrying Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) certification. This certification means the wood and products were harvested, processed, and tracked according to established environmental and sourcing standards.

Industry observers note that patios are another popular garden feature, and while I appreciate a nicely installed patio made with concrete, new pavers, or bricks, there are some other options available. It is key to consider the permeability of our pavement selections as challenges of runoff and erosion come into play.

Permeable pavers, open-grid pavers, and some types of pervious concrete can allow water to pass through the surface and into underlying layers, helping reduce runoff when properly installed and maintained.

Repurposing brick or other paving materials from another project is also an opportunity to add a vintage look and possibly save money. I have a client who obtained more than 4,000 free vitrified clay pavers from the early 1900s (used for streets!) that we used for his paths and patios, and they look fabulous. Reusing these durable materials also kept them in circulation rather than requiring newly manufactured pavers.

Don’t neglect to check out the wide range of energy-efficient lighting options for your landscape as well.

It has been revealed that I’ve also been involved with some rustic patios made of upcycled concrete pieces that were fitted together like puzzle pieces, the gaps filled with plants. Research “urbanite” patios and paths, and see the amazing results!

Industry observers note that it’s a great use of a common material that frequently ends up in our landfills. Crushed concrete is another useful material for paths. It can also be used as a base layer for paths and patios, provided it is suitable for the intended application. Again, local sourcing can reduce the carbon footprint associated with shipping and transportation.

Our reasons for supporting eco-friendly hardscaping decisions in our landscapes include, of course, preventing waste, conserving resources, and protecting our local and regional ecosystems and habitats.

While the convenience of buying readily available fresh materials may be appealing, taking the time to look into salvaged, recycled, locally sourced, and responsibly manufactured alternatives can yield equally attractive results.

According to recent reports, whether you’re planning a new patio, replacing an aging deck, or adding a garden path, find out what materials might already be available for reuse. Explore these opportunities!

Mark Dwyer owns Landscape Prescriptions by MD and is the garden manager for the Edgerton Hospital Healing Garden in Edgerton, Wisconsin. He previously served as director of horticulture at Rotary Botanical Gardens in Janesville, Wisconsin, for 21 years.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that earlier this week, I shared a look at the historic sunken garden connecting two homes built for sisters in Wilmette, Illinois.
  • Recent findings suggest that tucked away on Northwestern University’s campus, the Shakespeare Garden has been around for more than a century!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?”.

Perhaps he was hiding somewhere in the shade on that hot June day!

It has been revealed that earlier this week, I shared a look at the historic sunken garden connecting two homes built for sisters in Wilmette, Illinois. Today, we’re taking a look at another beautiful garden and a little Shakespearean history.

Recent findings suggest that tucked away on Northwestern University’s campus, the Shakespeare Garden has been around for more than a century! It all started in 1915, when the Garden Club of Evanston decided to create a garden to commemorate the 300th anniversary of Shakespeare’s death and celebrate the ties between England and America during World War I. They brought in renowned Danish-American landscape architect Jens Jensen to design the space, and by 1920, the club had completed planting a collection inspired by more than 50 plants mentioned in Shakespeare’s works. How neat! The garden was officially dedicated in 1930 and added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1988.

The Garden Club of Evanston still cares for the garden today, and it’s a wonderful little place to visit. Enjoy!

While wandering the shady paths at the back of the garden, I came across this natural doorway formed by the trees. What a beautiful view of the central lawn and sundial! Jensen wanted the formal garden to feel like a clearing in the woods, and I think he achieved just that.

Industry observers note that the garden measures just 70 by 100 feet and is made up of eight planting beds originally arranged in a formal knot-garden design. (If you’re not familiar with knot gardens, look them up! They’re amazing!) In 1990, English garden designer John Brookes recommended removing some of the boxwood (Buxus cvs., Zones 4–9) to make room for more perennials and a more relaxed planting style. He also had the sundial moved to the center to create a stronger focal point.

The garden underwent a renovation in 2016 to restore several of its historic features, including the wooden obelisks seen here, stone benches, and pathways. The project also included replacing declining plants to help preserve the original design.

My favorite view of the garden! Formally informal.

Jensen’s original planting list included everything from columbines (Aquilegia vulgaris, Zones 3–8) and violets (Viola spp., Zones 3–9) to poppies (Papaver somniferum, annual), peonies (Paeonia officinalis, Zones 4–8), and lavender (Lavandula angustifolia, Zones 5–8), all plants mentioned in Shakespeare’s writings. The plantings have changed over the years, but the garden still celebrates that connection.

Last, but certainly not least, this Elizabethan-style stone bench was installed in 1929, along with the garden’s memorial fountain. Nearly a century later, it’s still a beautiful spot to sit and enjoy the surroundings!

According to recent reports, the Shakespeare Garden is open to the public, and I highly recommend stopping by if you’re ever in the area! You can learn more about its history and plan your visit through the Garden Club of Evanston’s website.
