#113230. Tech Report: How to Design a Garden That Solves Problems and Invites You In

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1050 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Finegardening ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: How to Design a Garden That Solves Problems and Invites You In

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1050 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finegardening

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • People often ask how I approach the garden design process and what information I gather before developing a plan.
  • I like to create purpose-driven designs.
  • Design is all about solving problems and connecting clients to their gardens, usually beginning with a questionnaire to bring all those unspoken needs to light.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People often ask how I approach the garden design process and what information I gather before developing a plan. While every client and garden is different, I usually start with the same basic questions.

I like to create purpose-driven designs. For example, I’m often called on to solve a problem, even if it is simply “I have a latest house and a blank slate.” It may be just a section of the garden, the front yard, or something specific like repairing a garden after a new septic system installation or after a new house is built next door.

Design is all about solving problems and connecting clients to their gardens, usually beginning with a questionnaire to bring all those unspoken needs to light. Questions help people consider things they would not normally think about. As a result, these conversations define their needs and desires, helping me combine different elements into a cohesive design.

Industry observers note that the same approach applies to projects in my own garden. I don’t give myself a questionnaire, but I do ask myself the same questions. First, I assess the challenges, the location of the area in relation to the rest of the property, and the environmental conditions that will influence the planting.

According to recent reports, in a latest garden, the major goal is often screening. Most people want privacy to live their lives outside without having to see a neighboring house, road, commercial area, or vacant lot.

Industry observers note that privacy was one of the substantial considerations when planning my grass garden. There was no privacy between my property and the neighboring property. I could see my neighbors eat their dinner, watch them play with their grandchildren, and even see them argue. Their house was also too close to the property line, and in fact, their sidewalk was on my property. That was a problem.

Because the sidewalk was already there when I moved in, I had to incorporate it into my design, but I could still make it disappear visually.

I started out with some tall elements at the back of the bed to start the screening process. I positioned these plants so I could maintain them from my property without having branches extend over the property line. Keeping their mature size in mind also helped avoid potential conflicts with the neighboring property. Soft screens made of trees and tall shrubs (both evergreen and deciduous) offer privacy without creating a harsh, artificial boundary line.

Read More: 20 Unique Hedging Plant Options.

In a recent development, looking at the space, I could see a definite focal point within my property. With the neighbor behind me, the view naturally led the eye toward the water. Therefore, I designed a one-sided border rather than an island bed meant to be viewed from multiple directions. Making the border as deep as 20 feet in places gave me enough room to continue screening the neighboring property while also providing some sound buffering.

According to recent reports, understanding the environmental conditions was the next step. The back edge is on the north side of my property. The large trees and shrubs would not shade the rest of the bed. This meant the bed would be in full sun all day, all season long.

In a recent development, what a challenge for this PNW native who grew up mostly in the forest (or woods, as we called it). I had to learn about plants that liked full sun, drying winds, and dry soil so they could thrive. Rather than trying to re-create the shaded woodland conditions I knew best, I needed to work with what the site naturally offered.

Read More: Summer-Dry Gardening: A Visit to Beth Chatto’s Gravel Garden.

Growing up in the forest, I longed for wide-open sky and long views. Above all, I wanted to immerse myself in the garden. A long row of hedging plants that I could only look at wasn’t what I had in mind. I wanted to become part of the blowing, rustling movement of the grasses. While experiencing the plants, I also wanted to connect with insects, pollinators, birds, frogs, and even a few rabbits.

I consider the challenge met. The amount of wildlife activity surrounding me in the garden never ceases to amaze me. I feel as if I’m in a different world while surrounded by all the action and movement of the grasses and perennials, far away from major cedar trees, moss, and ferns. Sun, wind, fragrant flowers, and the smell of warm earth are all-encompassing there.

Recent findings suggest that even during the winter, this garden pulls me out, bundled up and coffee in hand, to see what is happening. Early spring bulbs push through the soil, mice shelter under the evergreen sedges, and birds search for a breakfast of grass seeds and gather bits and pieces to build fresh nests.

The ultimate goal of any designer is finding the right outdoor elements to pull people outside and connect them with nature. Those elements are individual to each client. They could be an eating area, outdoor kitchen, hot tub, play area, pond, fountain, or hidden sitting area. Maybe the goal is plant-driven, with a vegetable garden, cutting garden, or collection of conifers.

When these features are thoughtfully integrated with immersive, naturalistic plantings, the result is an outdoor space that invites people to experience their gardens throughout the year.

Susan Calhoun is the owner and principal designer of Plantswoman Design in Bainbridge Island, Washington.

  • In Minneapolis, our growing season may be short, but we squeeze every drop of joy out of our small urban garden!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that hi GPOD! I’ve recently gotten a few emails from readers asking about submissions they entered through the website link at the end of every GPOD. Unfortunately, I haven’t received any submissions through the form in quite a while. I’m not sure what the problem is, but hopefully there will be a resolution soon. In the meantime, you can submit your photos and captions through the email linked below instead.

It has been revealed that today we’re touring Arianne and Micah’s garden in Minneapolis, Minnesota. And while looking through their latest photos, I kept forgetting that I was looking at a garden in the Midwest! Arianne has shared their garden with us before, and I’m excited to see what they’ve been growing this year. Here’s Arianne:.

In Minneapolis, our growing season may be short, but we squeeze every drop of joy out of our small urban garden! It’s packed with flowers I start from seed—like zinnias, cosmos, statice, strawflower, celosia, and amaranth—along with overwintered dahlias. I love cutting fresh bouquets to gift to friends, family, and coworkers. When we’re not admiring the blooms, my husband is cooking outdoors—making wood-fired pizzas, wok dishes, and hosting family birthday celebrations right in the heart of our cozy yard.

Arianne packs plenty of interest into the garden along in the front yard and along the curb strip. Plants in this section of the garden include dwarf purple smokebush, threadleaf bluestar (Amsonia hubrichtii, Zones 5–8), boxwood (Buxus cvs., Zones 4–9), lamb’s ear (Stachys byzantina, Zones 4–8), purpleleaf sand cherry (Prunus × cistena, Zones 2–8), coreopsis (Coreopsis cvs., Zones 3–9), alliums (Allium cvs., Zones 3–9), sedum, and artemisia. It’s a great mix of foliage colors and textures even when everything isn’t in bloom.

In a recent development, I love the placement of the patio and pathway. It’s a really useful design technique for maximizing every square inch of a small garden while still leaving plenty of room for outdoor living.

Absolutely gorgeous section of the garden! This is where we really start to feel like we’re in the tropics. ‘Mars Madness’ hardy hibiscus (Hibiscus ‘Mars Madness’, Zones 4–9) has all the tropical drama while still being hardy enough for a Minneapolis winter. And it’s hard to miss those giant cannas and the colorful foliage on the coleus. I love all the red blooms too!

In a recent development, one of Arianne’s fabulous container combinations features Tropicanna Gold canna (Canna ‘Mactro’, Zones 8–11), purple shield (Strobilanthes dyerianus, annual), begonias (Begonia cvs., annual), flowering kale (Brassica oleracea, annual), and parrot’s beak (Lotus berthelotii, annual). So much of the color and interest here comes from foliage!

There is so much to look at in this section of the garden! Those variegated geranium leaves are striking, and I could go on and on about Arianne’s use of color and texture. The apple tree surrounded by all these ornamentals is an unexpected but lovely touch.

Just around the corner from the photo above. Another gorgeous tropical container, and ‘Blue Shadow’ fothergilla (Fothergilla × intermedia ‘Blue Shadow’, Zones 5–8) grows on the left in this view.

Another view of the backyard borders. There are so many plants packed into this garden, you would never believe this is a small urban backyard. And, if my eyes are working correctly, I’d say that’s a clover lawn?!

Tall conifers create a fantastic privacy screen in this view. The garden really is its own secluded paradise.

A shady combination of hostas, ‘Banana Boat’ sedge (Carex siderosticha ‘Banana Boat’, Zones 4–9), painted fern, purple shield, coleus, and impatiens.

Industry observers note that zinnias, statice, amaranth, and overwintered dahlias are just some of the blooms that make their way into bouquets for friends, family, and coworkers. So pretty!

Thank you so much for sharing your garden with us again, Arianne! It’s always a treat to see what you and Micah are growing, and I think I could spend hours wandering around this garden and still find something newly introduced to admire.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hi GPOD! Today we’re heading to Hingham, Massachusetts, for some beautiful fall color from Nancy. Nancy sent in photos of the trees and shrubs winding down the season in her garden, along with one of the last flowers still hanging on.

This is our sugar maple (Acer saccharum, Zones 3–8) showing off its fall foliage before it drops its leaves to keep my gardens warm this winter.

My ‘Forest Pansy’ eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis ‘Forest Pansy’, Zones 5–9) is maroon most of the year until fall, when it turns a lovely yellow.

My paperbark maple (Acer griseum, Zones 4–8) has had a hard time coping with our summer droughts and water restrictions, but it looked a lovely red this fall.

Sources indicate that this is another native tree that many people are not familiar with, fringe tree (Chionanthus virginicus, Zones 4–9), which has fragrant white flowers hanging from its branches in late spring to early summer. As you can see, it also looks beautiful in its yellow fall foliage.

Industry observers note that in the front of this picture is a young sweetgum (Liquidambar styraciflua, Zones 5–9), which has spectacular red color in the fall and develops spiky seed balls as it matures. In the distance is a blackhaw viburnum (Viburnum prunifolium, Zones 3–9) showing its orange fall color.

‘Mount Airy’ fothergilla (Fothergilla ‘Mount Airy’, Zones 5–8) glows red and orange in front of fragrant abelia (Abelia mosanensis, Zones 4–8), whose fall color is beginning to fade. The abelia will charm us all again in spring with its fragrant blooms.

Recent findings suggest that sweetshrub (Calycanthus floridus, Zones 5–9) on the right has turned a lovely yellow. Amazingly, all three sweetshrubs shown here had the bark eaten off around every trunk by rabbits last winter, killing every one. They all grew back from the roots, showing just how resilient they are. On the left, ‘Mount Airy’ fothergilla is showing off its red fall foliage, and in back is ‘Alice’ oakleaf hydrangea (Hydrangea quercifolia ‘Alice’, Zones 5–9) with maroon fall foliage.

One of the only flowers left blooming is ‘Sheffield Pink’ chrysanthemum (Chrysanthemum ‘Sheffield Pink’, Zones 5–9), which complements the dark foliage of Diabolo ninebark (Physocarpus opulifolius ‘Monlo’, Zones 3–7) behind it.

Recent findings suggest that thanks for sharing your fall garden with us, Nancy! Nancy says she’s ready to wander the garden, make her list of what needs dividing in spring, and figure out what new plants need to be bought. Sounds like a good way to spend the off-season to me!

  • Given the attention his move has received, Yoo has written an op-ed for the Fresh York Post explaining his decision to choose Texas, and disputing any suggestion that he was driven out of Berkeley.
  • I'm leaving not because I feel driven out by Berkeley — anything but.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that professor John Yoo is leaving the law school at the University of California at Berkeley to join the School of Civic Leadership at the University of Texas at Austin. As I noted here, his departure means there will not be a single right-leaning professor teaching public law subjects at Berkeley--and no more than a handful (if that) at all of the UC schools combined.

Given the attention his move has received, Yoo has written an op-ed for the Fresh York Post explaining his decision to choose Texas, and disputing any suggestion that he was driven out of Berkeley.

I'm leaving not because I feel driven out by Berkeley — anything but.

In my three decades there I've enjoyed working, on an individual level, with spirited, ambitious students and challenging, innovative scholars.

I'm moving because Berkeley, like its peers, has declined from a daring, risk-taking center of higher learning to one that wallows contentedly in a monoculture of liberalism.

Yoo states the school has been obsessed with ethnic diversity while disregarding viewpoint diversity, and that this has eroded the institution's commitment to free speech and created an environment in which anti-semitism has taken root.

I've watched students and the usual agitators disrupt debates on affirmative action, spark pitched fights on Sproul Plaza and try to shout down distinguished scholars and thinkers (home of the Free Speech Movement, indeed).

Tolerance of such shenanigans was matched by intolerance of conservative or libertarian views on the faculty.

Industry observers note that berkeley has consistently rejected conservative scholars, no matter how well-qualified, well-published or widely cited. . . .

It has been revealed that one famous member of a revered Berkeley humanities department (always ranked among the nation's top three) once told me directly that he would never hire a conservative. . . .

Most student groups at Berkeley Law now boycott any event with a speaker who believes in Israel's right to exist.

For the first time in my 33 years at Berkeley I witnessed a heckler's veto, as protesters prevented a member of the Israeli Knesset from speaking — and top university officials stood idly by.

Students posted flyers depicting the dean of the law school — a liberal scholar with whom I rarely agree — feasting on human beings, then physically invaded his home while he hosted members of the graduating class, simply because he is Jewish.

Yoo argues that great universities should refocus their teaching on Western Civilization, so that the nation does not lose sight of the ideals upon which it was founded and the principles that provide the foundation for western prosperity.

The emergence of human reason in Greece and religious revelation in Jerusalem produced the free markets, natural rights, rule of law and democratic self-government that have made our astounding prosperity and power possible.

These ideals run directly counter to the poison running rampant on our campuses. . . .

Texas wants to restore Western civilization and the great books to the center of its curriculum — not to blindly agree with the past, but to understand and debate it.

I'm eager to join the Texans who want to defend free speech and thought, and to leave behind a California that rejects the West.

Recent findings suggest that hi GPOD! Yesterday we enjoyed some beautiful fall color in Nancy’s Massachusetts garden, and today we’re heading west to see what fall looked like in Colorado this year.

Sources indicate that bonnie took these photos in mid-November after an unusually long fall. While the trees certainly put on a show, Bonnie says the shrubs were the real stars this year. Here’s Bonnie:.

According to recent reports, colorado put on a spectacular fall color display this year. My garden was filled with so many vivid hues that I had to capture them in photos. Some years are more colorful than others, and this was certainly a good one! The standout colors came not from the trees, but from the shrubs.

Welcome to my fall garden! Just walk through the arch and see the colors beyond. ‘Forest Pansy’ eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis ‘Forest Pansy’, Zones 5–9) starts in spring with dark burgundy leaves, turns green by late summer, and finishes the season in bright yellow. I love this tree!

Recent findings suggest that other stars in my fall garden are the barberries, hydrangeas, dwarf smokebushes (Cotinus coggygria cvs., Zones 4–8), and spireas. Oh, and the Diabolo ninebark (Physocarpus opulifolius ‘Monlo’, Zones 3–7) in the back turned a lovely red this year.

Barberry, dwarf smokebush, and spireas in the back make a nice composition.

I’m in love with these ‘Annabelle’ smooth hydrangeas (Hydrangea arborescens ‘Annabelle’, Zones 3–9). They are all over my yard.

Another hydrangea vignette with viburnum, boxwood, and Japanese forest grass (Hakonechloa macra, Zones 5–9) in front.

I love the beautiful colors of this barberry.

Around the other side of our yard, the dwarf smokebush shines among the evergreens and the orange leaves of the mountain ash and honey locust (Gleditsia triacanthos, Zones 3–8) trees.

Looking toward the front yard, the dwarf smokebush steals the show!

Another view from the front yard.

A weeping Norway spruce (Picea abies, Zones 3–7) and barberry make a beautiful combination.

Recent findings suggest that thanks for sharing your beautiful fall garden with us, Bonnie! The trees are gorgeous, but I agree that the shrubs really stole the show this year.

I have lived in this house and garden for a little over a year. When I moved here, I worked hard to transplant many of my plants, and the garden continues to be a work in progress.

Delphinium (Delphinium cvs., Zones 3–7) with coleus (Coleus scutellarioides, annual).

Native swamp rose mallow (Hibiscus moscheutos, Zones 5–9) and zinnias.

Perennial begonia (Begonia grandis, Zones 6–9), a soft mahonia bush just planted this spring, and amaranth.

A watermelon my husband grew in our garden area created by a fresh stepped retaining wall.

A work in progress… I transplanted this hearts-a-bustin’ (Euonymus americanus, Zones 6–9) from a different spot where I originally had it. It was crowded in and now will be able to spread out.

It has been revealed that this celosia (Spicata group) actually grew from seeds of plants that were in a pot last summer. The ground in this area is where a tree used to be, and the roots are rotting and creating wonderful soft soil.

Thanks for sharing another patch from your garden, Connie! And I have to know: What variety of watermelon did your husband grow? It’s huge and oblong! I hope it was delicious. Looking forward to the next update! 🙂.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that hi GPOD! Longtime contributor Kielian is back today with another beautiful look at her garden in Hamilton, Montana. We’ve followed this garden through the seasons for years, and GPOD readers may even remember Kielian’s first autumn tour from more than a decade ago. Today she’s sharing what fall looks like on the ranch nearly 17 years into the garden’s evolution.

In the Bitterroot Valley of Montana, fall imparts her special light and changing colors to the ranch. The gardens are closing in on 17 years of beauty and, interestingly, have decided which design they like the most… on their own.

It has been revealed that my detailed blueprints and drawings of plantings have been changed by Mother Nature, who knows so much more than I do about proper placement. Birds deposit valuable seeds in areas I would never have approved of, and the failure of certain plants to survive makes room for those that forge ahead with gusto. Ahh, autumn, how delightful are your colors and resilience.

Late October in Montana: The ‘Pee Wee’ oakleaf hydrangeas (Hydrangea quercifolia ‘Pee Wee’, Zones 5–9) are showing off, and the ornamental pear tree was not going to be outdone.

The front garden early in the morning: Shadows enhance the color changes.

Industry observers note that the back deck was sprinkled with maple-tree graffiti. The linden tree boasted brilliant yellow, and a gorgeous crabapple by the pump house screamed for attention with bright red leaves.

A smokebush (Cotinus coggygria, Zones 4–8) and aspen tree drip with early morning rain.

A golden sunset scattered early October rays on quaking aspens (Populus tremuloides, Zones 1–6), enhanced by the Bitterroot Mountains as a backdrop.

Tessa came running along the path through early November changing leaves.

An ornamental pear tree with fading black-eyed Susans in front. Winter is on her way.

Thanks for sharing another season in your garden with us, Kielian! After seeing this garden in spring, summer, fall, and even covered in snow over the years, it’s hard to pick a favorite season. But that golden sunset over the pond with the Bitterroot Mountains in the distance certainly makes a strong case for fall!

📖 0% read

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that hey, garden gang! Longtime contributor Susan Warde is back today with a closer look at her garden in St. Paul, Minnesota. We’ve seen what the end of the season looks like in Susan’s garden before, but today she’s focusing on the smaller details that are easy to overlook this time of year.

I understand the reasons for not cutting down perennials and for letting leaves lie untouched over the winter, but it takes me about 10 weeks to clean up. I have a large garden, family commitments, unpredictable weather, and a limited number of yard-waste bags that our pickup service will take at one time. Ten weeks in the spring would put me into mid-June before I could get the weeds and overwintered mess under control.

It has been revealed that so I’ve been cleaning up, and the garden has been looking pretty bare recently, positively grim on overcast days. But during the process I was struck by small vignettes of beauty that stood out in an otherwise desolate landscape.

The underside of some Korean maple leaves (Acer pseudosieboldianum, Zones 4–8).

A ‘Northern Hi-Lights’ azalea (Rhododendron ‘Northern Hi-Lights’, Zones 4–7) with bright fall color… and buds that promise spring.

The seed head of ‘Guernsey Flute’ clematis (Clematis ‘Guernsey Flute’, Zones 4–9) that had a second late flowering.

One last blossom on a ‘Max Frei’ bloody cranesbill (Geranium sanguineum ‘Max Frei’, Zones 3–8).

Raindrops on columbine (Aquilegia cvs., Zones 3–8) leaves.

The yellowed leaves of a bulblet fern (Cystopteris bulbifera, Zones 3–8) that I’d overlooked during the cutting-down process.

A bee enjoys the very last plant in bloom, black cohosh (Actaea racemosa, Zones 3–8).

Evergreen Christmas fern (Polystichum acrostichoides, Zones 3–8) and moss.

I had never before looked closely at the bark of a blue beech (Carpinus caroliniana, Zones 3–9), which from a distance just looks taupe.

Five minutes before taking the photo, I’d cleaned out this birdbath—the one I leave available in winter, and then only on above-freezing days. The leaves are from a ‘North Wind’ maple (Acer × pseudosieboldianum ‘IslNW’, Zones 4–7).

Thanks for sharing these small moments from your garden, Susan! There are so many things to love about a garden, but I often find that the small details people tend to gloss over are even more reason to celebrate. There’s so much happening at once! You just have to look closely to see it. (:.

#113220. Tech Report: Keep Ducts Where They Belong

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2459 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Finehomebuilding ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Keep Ducts Where They Belong

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2459 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finehomebuilding

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that installing HVAC equipment and ductwork in unconditioned attics can increase energy costs, reduce comfort, and contribute to air leakage, condensation, mold growth, and indoor air quality problems.
  • For decades, houses have been built with forced-air ductwork and heating and cooling equipment in unconditioned attics.
  • Recent findings suggest that my organization, Aarow Building, has been building high-performance homes in Missouri for going on three decades now.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that installing HVAC equipment and ductwork in unconditioned attics can increase energy costs, reduce comfort, and contribute to air leakage, condensation, mold growth, and indoor air quality problems. Plenum trusses create dedicated spaces above ceilings for ductwork and other mechanical systems within the home’s conditioned envelope, helping maintain consistent ceiling heights while improving energy efficiency and durability. Successful implementation requires early coordination among builders, architects, HVAC designers, and truss manufacturers, along with carefully planned duct layouts and continuous, airtight control layers to prevent moisture problems and ensure long-term performance.

For decades, houses have been built with forced-air ductwork and heating and cooling equipment in unconditioned attics. The wide-open, easy-to-access attic space makes the practice common, convenient, and familiar for the framing and mechanical trades. But from a building-performance standpoint, it’s a terrible idea. Vented attics are extremely hot in summer and cold in winter, so every foot of duct placed in that location exposes the conditioned air within the ductwork to temperatures way beyond those inside the house.

Recent findings suggest that my organization, Aarow Building, has been building high-performance homes in Missouri for going on three decades now. We have a hot, humid climate and—like in many places—attic ductwork is common here, so we’ve seen plenty of examples of what can happen when you install HVAC equipment in an unconditioned space.

It has been revealed that for starters, the extreme temperature difference between the conditioned air inside the ducts and the temperature outside them results in a house that uses more energy and is more expensive to heat and cool compared to a house with an HVAC system inside the conditioned space. And the additional expense isn’t limited to operational costs. HVAC ducts and equipment in unconditioned spaces must have higher capacities to compensate for the adverse conditions where they’re located, meaning the systems are more expensive.

Higher costs are not the only downsides. Supply and return air leaks are common with HVAC systems in attics and are problematic from a building-durability and performance perspective. Supply leaks waste conditioned air and pressurize the attic, which depressurizes the house, causing additional air leakage in the conditioned space—and in extreme scenarios, backdrafting of combustion appliances.

Backdrafting can release carbon monoxide into the home, creating a serious risk of poisoning. There’s also a lot of water vapor in flue gasses, which can create humidity problems and mold growth. Equally common are return leaks that pull dusty, humid, or hot attic air into the heating or cooling system, negatively affecting energy efficiency, occupant comfort, and indoor air quality.

Industry observers note that air-conditioning supply ducts, which are cold, often become condensing surfaces. Condensing water can ruin finishes and lead to mold growth that may or may not be visible. Mold you can’t see can be especially problematic for sensitive individuals who might experience cold-like symptoms, asthma, or other respiratory problems. Similar problems can occur in cold climates when warm, conditioned air contacts cold spaces, creating condensation and potential mold problems. Even the most reliable HVAC system, when located outside the enclosure, can lead to comfort complaints and callbacks that are hard to diagnose and fix.

You can avoid all these problems by making room for HVAC ducts inside the house’s conditioned space during the design phase, before the house is built. The concept is not fresh—building scientists started advocating for ductwork within conditioned spaces in the late ’80s and early ’90s, and conscientious builders and designers paid attention. They developed methods for hiding ductwork in dropped hallway ceilings and in soffits that run along the tops of walls (see the drawings).

Recent findings suggest that these methods work—but from a design perspective, employing them can be tough on some homes. I’ve found that soffits in bedrooms are almost always unwanted by designers and clients. I think the best way to hide ducts, both substantial and small, is to place them in ceiling chases using plenum trusses.

It has been revealed that my first exposure to plenum trusses came from architect Steve Baczek. For a period, Steve was working with a production builder in the Southwest United States that offered a comfort guarantee for every home they built. One of the ways they ensured comfort was by keeping the HVAC system inside the building envelope. In some parts of the house, Steve hid ductwork in soffits, but he also used plenum trusses in places where soffits were impractical. The idea of using plenum trusses stuck with me.

It has been revealed that we eventually began using plenum trusses in some of our builds for the same reasons as Steve: greater comfort, efficiency, and building durability. In 2017, our manufacturer made the decision that ductwork and HVAC equipment would be installed inside the conditioned enclosure whenever possible. In homes with a conditioned attic, the solution is easy. The ducts can simply live in the attic. The same is true when we have a conditioned crawlspace or basement available for distribution.

In a recent development, many of the homes we build, however, are slab-on-grade with a vented attic above them. Those homes require another strategy, and plenum trusses have become one of our preferred solutions. They allow us to maintain consistent ceiling heights throughout the house while still providing a dedicated space for ductwork and other mechanical systems inside the building envelope. The result gives us the architectural appearance we want without compromising the mechanical strategy, occupant comfort, or energy efficiency.

Industry observers note that plenum trusses are engineered with an open space free of chords and braces that becomes a cavity for ducts, pipes, and refrigeration lines running perpendicular to the trusses. This plenum cavity is lined with an air-impermeable material, typically wood sheathing or drywall for airtightness. Ducts can also be run in angled plenums or in an airtight plenum space made between two trusses, as seen in the photos below.

Parallel Plenum: In this space, eight girder trusses have an opening that allows a duct to pass through them and then turn 90° into a plenum space built on-site from taped sheathing between two of the girder trusses. Both site-built and engineered plenum spaces need a continuous air barrier—in this case, taped sheathing—to prevent air movement through the plenum space.

It has been revealed that angled Plenum: To get the conditioned air to its intended registers most efficiently, the main plenum on this project is angled and installed within 10 individually engineered trusses. Each truss has the plenum space offset a few inches from the previous truss’s plenum space, creating the angled plenum. It took about an hour with the truss designer to plan this layout.

Strapped Ceiling: Once the ductwork is installed and sealed and other mechanicals are in place, the ceiling is strapped with 2×4 furring for securing the finished drywall ceiling.

It has been revealed that A plenum truss offers a way to design a house’s framing around the mechanical systems, rather than squeezing ductwork into whatever leftover space is available. In simple terms, the bottom chord of a plenum truss is notched with a framed rectangle above, creating a dedicated service cavity, or chase, above the finished ceiling. Importantly, the chase is within the building enclosure, beneath the air, insulation, and vapor control layers—unlike an unconditioned attic, which is essentially outside the building. In addition to ductwork, the plenum space can also house electrical and low-voltage wiring, pipes, and other mechanical systems while keeping them inside the conditioned space of the home.

The key point is that the chase is designed, not discovered. You can’t build the chase with field alterations after the trusses arrive. By then, the rooflines, heel heights, load paths, bearing points, ceiling planes, and mechanical layout are already largely locked in. A plenum-truss strategy can only work when the builder, architect, mechanical designer, and truss supplier are involved early on and work together. In my experience, the biggest challenge has been the truss design. Nearly every builder or designer I know who uses plenum trusses has encountered some degree of resistance or hesitation from a truss manufacturer, which I think is understandable. We are asking the truss designer to create something more complicated than a conventional roof truss while accommodating structural loads, duct dimensions, roof geometry, bearing locations, and the other constraints of the building.

Recent findings suggest that the best results we have had come from working directly with the truss designer early in the process. Whenever possible, we sit down with the designer and work through the layout before the trusses are finalized. An extra hour spent with a truss designer is how you end up with a plenum large enough to fit and efficiently route the ducts while framing the complicated rooflines typical of the custom homes we build. Modern truss-design software makes it relatively easy to look at the proposed truss geometry and determine if the plenum will be big enough and correctly positioned for efficiently routing ducts that are the right size.

Sources indicate that plenum ceilings use furred-down framing or drywall-suspension systems to lower the entire ceiling. The system requires a second air barrier above the furred-down section(s), adding significant cost and complexity to the whole ceiling assembly and not just the plenum service cavity.

Lowered ceilings refer to a section of lowered ceiling (often in hallways), and were pioneered by building scientists as a way to keep ductwork in the conditioned space. The system is less expensive than dropping an entire ceiling, but many clients find the lowered portion of ceiling makes the hallway or other space feel oppressive or confining.

In a recent development, wall-to-ceiling soffits provide a space between the ceiling and the top of built-in cabinetry. Unfortunately, the design is often limited to concealing small ducts, and clients and designers often object to soffits outside the kitchen, especially when they obstruct a view or look like an afterthought.

Sources indicate that conditioned attics bring the insulation, air-control, and vapor-control layers to the roof sheathing, typically with spray foam on the underside of the roof sheathing. But insulating an entire attic with spray foam is expensive, and conditioned attics add a lot of space that must be temperature-controlled, increasing costs over time.

According to recent reports, once the house design is finalized, the next step is to determine where the ducts and equipment need to go. That means the HVAC design must be figured out before the trusses are ordered. The air-handler location, trunk lines, branch runs, register locations, return ducts, and grilles need to be finalized during the design process. A real duct layout matters. A rectangular box on a strategy marked “mechanical” is not enough, so we engage our mechanical design team early in the process and make sure the duct size and routing is specified in their HVAC design. Leaving the duct sizing and routing to whoever demonstrates up on installation day is never the right approach.

It has been revealed that once the duct layout is understood, the truss designer can design the truss framing to accommodate it. The chase needs to be deep and wide enough for the ductwork and anything else other trades require in the plenum space. It also needs to provide reasonable access for the people doing the work. If a duct must be bent, crushed, or forced around a framing member, the truss and/or HVAC design has failed. This is where builders need to be assertive in preconstruction. It’s not enough to simply ask whether the ductwork will fit—the HVAC designers should be able to identify on the intends where it will fit. By the end of the design process, the framing blueprint, mechanical plan, and truss drawings must agree with one another.

A plenum truss only improves building and HVAC performance if the service cavity is within the home’s conditioned enclosure, without any gaps in the control layers. The air-barrier location has to be clear, which can be verified using what building scientist Joe Lstiburek and architect Steve Baczek describe as the “red pen test.” You should be able to trace the home’s entire air barrier location on the looks without lifting a red pen. If the ceiling drywall is the primary air barrier and vapor-control layer, then the plenum needs to be detailed so the ceiling drywall connects to the drywall or sheathing surrounding the plenum cavity, keeping the air- and vapor-control layers continuous. In most cases, this means the plenum is drywalled inside, ducts are installed and sealed, and then ceiling drywall is installed below the plenum, creating a flat ceiling with hidden ductwork above.

We use Zip System sheathing as our air control layer in the plenum space and on the rest of the building enclosure. Our framing crews install and tape the sheathing in the plenum space as part of their framing contract. The material might cost a little more than a drywall air barrier, but we find that having the framers install the air barrier works better with job sequencing than having the drywallers at the project twice, first to install and tape the plenum drywall and a second time to drywall the rest of the house. Whether you use drywall or taped sheathing, the takeaway is the same: All three sides (sides and cap) of the plenum, and where it meets the ceiling drywall, must be airtight.

According to recent reports, the enclosure must also be airtight for vapor control, as most water that condenses on building surfaces and in cavities leading to mold and damage is the result of water vapor carried by air leaks that condenses on cold surfaces. Condensation can occur if the plenum space is not properly sealed from air movement, so you need a continuous air control layer in the plenum space and throughout the rest of the building for effective air and vapor control.

There’s no question that plenum trusses require more preconstruction planning than installing ducts and air handlers in unvented attics, and they typically add to the cost of a truss package. But the upfront planning and additional costs should be weighed against the cost of comfort complaints, wasted energy dollars, mold risk, and the labor involved with sealing penetrations and insulating ducts and HVAC equipment in unvented attics. Keeping ducts and HVAC equipment out of unconditioned spaces makes longer-lasting, more comfortable houses, which makes the additional effort and expense a smart investment for our clients.

Sources indicate that — Jake Bruton is the president of Aarow Builders in Columbia, Mo. Photos by the author. Drawings by Dan Thornton.

Second Amendment Roundup: AR-15 Film Redux.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (779 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Smith released his latest 85-minute film discussing the operations and mechanics of modern firearms, including semiautomatic rifles such as the popular AR-15 rifle.
  • That federal judges are now reviewing Internet videos to learn about firearms is hardly surprising.
  • As I previously wrote, I had the pleasure of introducing the "AR-15 Primer" film.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last week, Professor Mark W. Smith released his latest 85-minute film discussing the operations and mechanics of modern firearms, including semiautomatic rifles such as the popular AR-15 rifle. The film, titled "Firearms and the AR-15 Rifle: A Primer for the Bench and Bar," can be found on YouTube here and on Rumble. It has already been viewed over 23,000 times since its release only days ago. The film is broken down into 25 segments so a viewer can jump from topic to topic.

That federal judges are now reviewing Internet videos to learn about firearms is hardly surprising. A few weeks ago Judge Doris Pryor of the Seventh Circuit made reference to this during oral argument in a constitutional fight over the legality of Illinois's suppressor ban. In the consolidated cases of Anderson v. Raoul and Morse v. Raoul, argued October 28, 2026, she acknowledged that she has watched videos in preparing for oral argument. The oral argument audio recording is here with Judge Pryor's comment at the 25:04-25:23 mark.

As I previously wrote, I had the pleasure of introducing the "AR-15 Primer" film. From there, Rick Vasquez (a former ATF firearm technician and U.S. Marine ordnance officer) takes the spotlight explaining the mechanical operation of today's AR-15 rifle and its typical features.

But there is another vital aspect of the film that is worth noting. And that is the impressive animations found within the film that help educate legal professionals and the general public about the internal and related operations of the AR-15 (and most modern semi-automatic rifles).

The animations found throughout the film are informative for those learning about firearm mechanics. Here are a few of the noteworthy ones:.

There is an excellent 2-minute animation illustrating how gas-operated semiautomatic rifles internally deploy the rapidly-expanding gases from the firing of a shot to do two things: first, to send a projectile (the bullet) down the barrel and, second, to prepare the rifle to fire the next round of ammunition. This is called autoloading. This dual use of the gases from firing a single shot is generally not understood or appreciated by those newly introduced to firearms technology, but the film's animation makes it clear. This animation also clarifies that autoloading does not mean automatic fire (like one sees with a M16 machine gun). The animation can be seen at the 14:58 to 17:58 mark of the film.

It has been revealed that the film also does a nice job demonstrating the physical reality of recoil by illustrating how the features of an AR-15 like the straight line stock, the buffer spring/buffer tube, and the muzzle brake help to minimize recoil allowing for a more comfortable and effective shooting experience. The 28:09 to 28:22 mark has a nice illustration of the straight-line stock while the 28:28 to 28:59 mark illustrates the role of the buffer and buffer spring in minimizing uncomfortable recoil. The 27:59 to 28:07 mark shows an animation illustrating what constitutes recoil from the firing of a rifle.

Industry observers note that the film also effectively uses animation to illustrate the difference between scopes, red dot optics, and iron sights. A scope magnifies the target making it appear closer than it really is; a red dot optic helps the user aim the rifle using an electronic dot without magnification; and iron sights entail aligning a front post with a rear sight. The 1:00:53 to 1:01:18 mark illustrates these differences.

According to recent reports, animation also helps viewers understand that the barrel of a semiautomatic rifle gets hot when the rifle is fired due to the internal gas explosion that results from firing a round. The film's animation demonstrates the rifle barrel heating up and demonstrates the value of handguards (often called "barrel shrouds" in legislation) to protect the user of the rifle. The 46:24 to 46:33 mark illustrates a barrel heating up as the rifle is shot.

It has been revealed that the film's use of animations to explain the difference between a bullet and a cartridge is also worth mentioning. Lawyers (and even some judges) use those terms interchangeably, but they mean very different things. The 1:10:12 to 1:11:08 mark illustrates the four components (primer, gun power, case and bullet) of a modern ammunition cartridge.

Industry observers note that it has been said that the late President Harry Truman embraced the thought, "I am from Missouri so you have to show me." Well, Professor Smith's fresh film on firearm mechanics works hard to "show" (through animations, illustrations and images) the internal mechanics and features of AR-15 semiautomatic rifles. And I suspect the bench and the bar will be the better for it.

#113218. Fiber-Cement Plank Repair

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (886 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Finehomebuilding ↗ Open Full Page

Fiber-Cement Plank Repair

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (886 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finehomebuilding

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I need to remove 12 courses of blind-nailed 5-1/4-in.-wide fiber-cement lap siding with a 4-in.
  • It’s challenging to remove blind-nailed fiber-cement lap siding, but patience and an extra set of hands make removing and reinstalling the planks easier.
  • Recent findings suggest that first, mark out the damaged area with painter’s tape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I need to remove 12 courses of blind-nailed 5-1/4-in.-wide fiber-cement lap siding with a 4-in. exposure to repair a 5-ft. by 5-ft. section of wall behind it. I’d like to reinstall the old siding without it looking like a repair. What’s the best way to remove fiber-cement lap siding without damaging the planks? How can I make removal and reinstallation less noticeable?

It’s challenging to remove blind-nailed fiber-cement lap siding, but patience and an extra set of hands make removing and reinstalling the planks easier.

Recent findings suggest that first, mark out the damaged area with painter’s tape. You’ll have to remove full pieces of siding for the repair, so look for the nearest butt joints between individual planks to the left and right of the taped area. Mark the joints in every course of the taped repair area. Plank joints are generally staggered by two studs in successive courses—32 in. or 48 in., depending on the stud spacing. If you’re lucky, the repair area will fit within one 12-ft. plank, so you’ll need to remove just one plank per course between the nearest joints. More likely, you’ll need to remove two. This takes more time, but the removal process is the same.

The first plank is the hardest to remove. Start with the uppermost course in the area you marked out and gently pry up the overlying plank far enough to locate the nails. Then mark the nail locations with small pieces of tape on the overlying course. The butt joints to the left and right of the plank may have been caulked. If so, carefully cut through the sealant with a utility knife.

When fiber-cement planks are 8 in. or wider, you can lift the bottom edge far enough to pry out the nails from the plank below by slipping a thin flat bar under that plank and up to the shank of the nail. Gently pry the plank up slightly and then remove the flat bar. Press down on the top edge of the plank so the nail head stands proud of the surface, then set the flat bar under the nail head and pry it out.

Industry observers note that prying up narrower planks to pull 2-in. or longer nails often breaks the plank, so in these situations I use a thin cutting tool to cut the nails holding the plank—the Malco Hidden Nail Cutter is made for this job, though you can also use a reciprocating saw with a long metal-cutting blade. Set a 1-ft.-sq. piece of PVC or coil stock under the flat bar to avoid scratching the finish, gently lift the plank up about ¼ in. at each blind nail location, and use the Malco tool or recip saw to cut the nails. Don’t pry too much or you’ll break the top edge of the overlying plank. As you cut the nails, have a helper hold one end of the plank so you can control its removal and be careful sliding the plank downward so the cut-off nails don’t scratch the plank beneath.

It has been revealed that with the first plank out of the way, most of the nails holding the next plank down are exposed. Pull the exposed nails using the flat bar method: insert the flat bar between the plank and the wall sheathing at the nail location and pry against the wall; once the nail is broken free and raised 1/4 in., push the top of the plank back against the wall so the nail head is proud, and finish pulling the nail with the flat bar. Cut any blind nails that remain before removing the plank.

It has been revealed that continue working down, removing planks left and right as close to the taped-out area as possible. Remove the cut nails from the planks so they don’t scratch the siding during handling, and label the planks so you can reinstall them in the same locations.

After you make your wall repair, install a fresh piece of water-resistive barrier (WRB) taped along its perimeter to the existing WRB and tuck its top under the existing WRB to shed water. Then reinstall the planks in reverse sequence. I install new nails in the old holes, using ring-shank nails with a slightly larger diameter than the originals for a secure grip. At the ends of planks where they slide beneath an overlying course, you’ll have to face-nail. Make sure the nail penetrates through the overlap at the underlying and overlying planks near where the blind nail used to be.

It has been revealed that work your way up the wall until you reach the last plank that will slip beneath the existing plank at the top of the repaired area, then face-nail the last reinstalled plank. Face nails can be left exposed and touched up with color-matching paint, but they will be noticeable compared to the blind-nailed siding on the rest of the wall. You can somewhat hide the heads by countersinking them: Make recesses with a drill-mounted countersink and then putty and paint the heads so they’re less obvious. Don’t try hammering the nail heads below the siding surface because you’ll break the fiber cement and the nails won’t hold well.

Industry News: Air Barrier for an Elevated Home

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (606 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finehomebuilding

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’m about to build a house on the coast in Charleston, S.C.
  • It’s wise to consider inward vapor drive in humid climates like Charleston.
  • Sources indicate that there are a few ways to prevent this.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’m about to build a house on the coast in Charleston, S.C. (Climate Zone 3A). It’s elevated on wood pilings and the space under the house is open to the outdoors, enclosed only with louvered panels between the pilings. I have most of the enclosure details nailed down, but I haven’t determined the best way to air-seal and insulate the open floor trusses above the pilings. My biggest concern is hot, humid air from below reaching the underside of the air-conditioned subfloor and condensing on the surface. What’s the best strategy to insulate and air-seal the underside of an elevated coastal home?

It’s wise to consider inward vapor drive in humid climates like Charleston. When the outdoor dew point is higher than the air-conditioned indoor temperature, there’s going to be a strong moisture drive from the outside toward the home’s interior, which allows water to accumulate in the materials below the flooring. Prolonged wetting can lead to rotted framing, mold problems, and damaged flooring, along with damage to other materials in contact with the floor.

Sources indicate that there are a few ways to prevent this. One option is to place a vapor-retarding insulation layer—spray foam—right below the subfloor. The outside (bottom) of the foam will be close enough to the outdoor temperature that water won’t condense on the surface, and the foam will substantially block moisture from moving through it. Provided no ductwork is run in the floor, it’s a way to get decent air-sealing, and the cost is reasonable as well.

According to recent reports, that remarked, I don’t like to use spray foam across an entire floor—it’s risky to install and full of questionable chemicals. Another option is to create a conditioned space within the floor system. The challenge is air-sealing around the posts, beams, and structural hardware that hold up the house and the plumbing and electrical lines in this area. Plus, you’ll have to condition the space, which requires additional HVAC work. This can be simple (like adding a supply register and a path back to the house) or pretty involved (running ductwork down walls to reach the underfloor space).

According to recent reports, my third and preferred option is to create an airtight, vapor-retarding layer across the bottom of the floor trusses. A layer of XPS or foil-faced polyiso (don’t use EPS, it’s too vapor-open) across the bottom of the whole floor will help slow vapor drive into the floor system and bring practical benefits like easier air-sealing and a little additional insulation. In Climate Zone 3A, turn to the International Residential Code (IRC) Table 806.5 in the section on roof ventilation for guidance on the R-value needed, since the floor system will have insulation levels comparable to roofs. The table calls for 1/2 in. of rigid insulation. Using the calculation procedure in the table footnotes indicates a higher level (in the 11/2-in. range) might be less risky, assuming you are completely filling a 12-in. to 16-in. floor-truss cavity with blown-in cellulose or fiberglass, which will be more than the code-required R-38 when the table was developed. Cover the foam board with fiberglass-faced drywall sheathing or plywood. Air-­sealing will still be complex given the elevated construction, and attention will need to be paid to the rim joist/perimeter (spray foam works in this area, as shown in the drawing). But, this system would really slow vapor movement throughout the floor system.

#113215. Latest Update: Finding the Right Clients

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2387 w)

Latest Update: Finding the Right Clients

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2387 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finehomebuilding

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I spend a lot of time talking with builders who tell me they don’t really do marketing.
  • My first response is usually that this is a good thing.
  • Recent findings suggest that but I have also seen construction companies reach a point where the business landscape has changed, and reputation alone is not leading to the right clients.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I spend a lot of time talking with builders who tell me they don’t really do marketing. Usually they say it with pride: “We’ve never had to. All of our work comes from word of mouth.”.

My first response is usually that this is a good thing. If you’ve spent years building a firm where past clients, architects, and trade partners keep sending work your way, you’ve built something valuable. In construction, reputation matters, and that kind of trust is earned over time. I would never tell a builder to replace that with advertising.

Recent findings suggest that but I have also seen construction companies reach a point where the business landscape has changed, and reputation alone is not leading to the right clients. Good builders often struggle because the right people don’t know they exist.

The phone may still be ringing, but the work coming in doesn’t always match where the organization wants to go next. The business has evolved, but what people know about it hasn’t necessarily evolved with it.

Those are the moments when someone usually indicates, often a little reluctantly, “I guess we need to do some marketing.” That may indeed be the case. But I think there is a simpler and more useful way to frame the problem: Are you known for the work you actually want to do? That is where I would start.

I’ve spent more than 20 years helping businesses and organizations grow, evolve, and connect with the people they want to reach, from owning and running a design and marketing agency to leading a destination marketing organization and working across marketing, branding, organizational leadership, consulting, and coaching. Today, as director of marketing and a business consultant with HELM Construction Solutions, I bring those experiences together in my work with builders, helping them think about where their business is going, the work they want more of, and what makes them different.

Sit across the table with an experienced builder and you quickly understand what makes them different. But if you haven’t had that conversation, how would you know? I see this all the time: Some of the most valuable things about a construction organization live almost entirely in the owner’s head. The challenge is making more of that knowledge visible.

According to recent reports, before I talk with a builder about websites, social media, advertising, or anything else that might get labeled “marketing,” I want to understand the business they are trying to build. What kind of work would they happily do again? Which projects are profitable? Which projects make the crew proud? Which clients trust the process? Where do they want to work? Who do they want to work alongside? What do they want the organization to look like in five years? And—just as important—what do they want less of?

That last question can be surprisingly provocative. Construction companies are often encouraged to think about growth only in terms of more: more projects, more employees, more revenue, more leads. But growth doesn’t always mean more projects. Sometimes it means being more intentional about the work you take on.

I’ll ask why a builder does something a certain way, and suddenly we’re deep into a story about a detail, a process, or a hard-earned lesson that changed how they work. Those stories are usually where the good stuff is, and where what makes a tech giant different becomes clear.

In a recent development, at this point, a lot of decisions get easier. You don’t need to reach everybody. You just need to become more visible to the people who value that kind of work.

It has been revealed that if you aren’t sure how to identify the right types of projects for your business, I often suggest looking backward before looking forward. Choose three to five projects from the last few years that you would happily do again. Think about the jobs where the fit was right—the client trusted you, the work suited the strengths of your crew, the project was financially healthy, and the architect or designer was collaborative. Problems came up, as they always do, but the team solved them together rather than turning on one another. When the project ended, you were proud not only of what you built but of how you built it.

Industry observers note that then ask a simple question: How did that project find us? You may discover that the same architect appears several times. Maybe a handful of past clients have been quietly sending people your way for years. Perhaps one designer, Realtor, supplier, or fellow builder keeps connecting you to projects that are an unusually good fit. Those patterns matter. They show you where to focus your time and attention. And when you’re trying to become known somewhere new, that kind of focus becomes even more notable.

For example, Sycamore Builders in western North Carolina has strong experience with architect-led custom homes in mountain communities. But as the company looks to expand into nearby markets, it faces a familiar challenge: Reputation is local.

Industry observers note that in some of those communities, builders have been around for generations. Their trucks are familiar. Realtors and architects know them. Their projects are part of the landscape. That familiarity has been built over years. You cannot advertise your way into a 25-year relationship.

Recent findings suggest that so Sycamore is taking a patient approach by building relationships with architects and Realtors, sharing more of the stories behind its work, and showing up consistently in a few specific communities. The goal isn’t a flood of calls. One or two well-aligned new builds a year can make a ­meaningful difference.

Recent findings suggest that if the word marketing makes you want to stop reading, forget about marketing for a minute. Take an hour with your business partner, project manager, or someone who knows your organization well and work through these questions. Let your answers guide you in pinpointing the type of work you want to find. Once you do, you won’t need to network every week, post every day, or constantly revision your website. Pick a few actions that fit your business, and keep doing them.

What work do people call you for—and what work do you wish people called you for?

Recent findings suggest that be honest with yourself. Is the work you’re doing now the work you want to be doing? If not, that’s your starting point.

What are five projects you’d do again tomorrow?

What made those projects good for the client, the crew, and the business? Writing the answers down can help you determine the type of work you want to do more of.

How did each of those projects find you?

Recent findings suggest that maybe it was a past client, an architect, a builder, a Realtor, a jobsite sign, a Google search, or something else. Don’t guess—find out. Then you can use those same methods to find similar projects in the future.

Who is connected to the work you want?

Industry observers note that make a list of the Realtors, architects, designers, and trade partners who are connected to the kinds of projects and clients you want more of, using your favorite projects as a guide. Who do you already know? Who consistently connects you to good-fit work? Who would you like to build a stronger relationship with?

How can you stay connected to those people?

Could you invite someone to a jobsite, meet for coffee, share an interesting project over email, attend an industry event, or simply check in occasionally? Staying in touch helps potential partners remember you and your business when the right project comes along.

When someone looks you up, can they see what you want to be known for?

Do your website and social media show the types of projects you want to do? Are you telling the stories behind that work and making your expertise visible? The clearer you are about the work you want, the easier it is for the right clients and partners to recognize that you’re the right fit.

This is usually the point where someone notes, “Carrie, I have houses to build. I can’t spend all my time updating a website, posting on social media, meeting architects for coffee, and telling project stories.”.

That’s fair, and I don’t want you to. Go back to what you learned about your best projects, and choose two or three things you can realistically keep doing to continue getting this sort of work. For example, maybe that means staying connected to a small group of architects and adding a strong project story to your website every few months.

It has been revealed that then pay attention to what happens. Ask every fresh caller how they heard about you, notice which relationships lead to good-fit projects, and see whether the work coming through the door starts to look more like the work you want.

Recent findings suggest that for example, longtime high-performance builder Steve DeMetrick of DeMetrick Housewrights has spent more than two decades developing a reputation for building homes that demonstrate thoughtful craftsmanship, durability, and energy-efficiency. Most of his work has come through referrals. He has deep expertise, strong relationships, and plenty of experience. He is not trying to make the phone ring more.

Recent findings suggest that in fact, when we started talking about where he wants the firm to go next, his answer was almost the opposite of what we typically associate with growth. He wants to slow down. He wants fewer projects at a time, larger scope, deeper involvement with each client, earlier collaboration with architects, and more opportunity to use the knowledge he has accumulated over decades.

The more we talked, the clearer it became that high-performance construction is only part of what makes his firm valuable. What really stands out is how he approaches the whole process—bringing design, budget, and scope together early and getting everyone working together sooner. That can lead to better decisions, fewer surprises, and a better experience for everyone involved. But that type of value is a lot harder to advertise on the side of a truck.

In a recent development, the goal isn’t simply to tell more people that DeMetrick Housewrights builds high-performance homes. It is to make more of Steve’s thinking visible, to tell the stories behind projects, to explain why he approaches preconstruction the way he does, and to give potential clients and collaborators a better sense of what it is actually like to work with him. The point isn’t to create content for the sake of content. It is to help people see expertise that is already there.

I’ve seen the same thing with Bell Street Builders in Maine, an employee-owned cooperative that does thoughtful restoration and renovation work around Portland and Casco Bay, including historic homes, architect-driven projects, and coastal and island construction. Those projects come with the kinds of challenges experienced builders know well: older structures that reveal surprises, coastal exposure, difficult logistics, complicated sequencing, and the need to make decisions carefully when clients may be living elsewhere.

According to recent reports, when I worked on Bell Street’s strategic direction, one theme kept reappearing: Bell Street knows old buildings. This is much more useful than generically saying the company does “quality construction.”.

Sources indicate that if you own a 100-year-old house in Portland and are about to open walls that may be hiding decades of concerns, you want a builder who understands what they’re looking at and can respond without turning every surprise into a crisis. If you’re an architect working on that house, you want a builder who can solve problems collaboratively and respect the building while still moving the project forward.

It has been revealed that bell Street did not need to become known to every homeowner in southern Maine. The better opportunity was to become more recognizable for the work the company does best and in the places where it wants to do more of it. That meant making sure its website and social channels revealed more of its historic work and the stories behind complex projects, staying connected with architects and designers who work on those kinds of homes, and building relationships in priority communities such as Portland’s West End, Foreside communities, and the Casco Bay islands.

Becoming recognizable doesn’t have to mean constantly creating something newly introduced. One good project can go a long way. Document the challenges during construction, photograph the finished work, explain what the team had to solve, and share that story on a website, social media, or directly with architects and past clients who may know someone planning a similar project.

According to recent reports, I genuinely appreciate builders’ resistance to marketing. It usually stems from a belief that the work should matter most. I think so too.

A clever website cannot make up for poor craftsmanship. Advertising cannot replace trust, and social media cannot substitute for treating clients well, running a good jobsite, respecting trade partners, or standing behind what you build. Your reputation still has to be earned.

Sources indicate that once you’ve earned it, however, there is nothing wrong with helping it travel. That doesn’t require becoming a marketer. It simply means being a little more intentional about making the work, knowledge, and people behind your firm visible.

Sources indicate that and there is a benefit beyond finding the kinds of projects you want. The same things that help clients, architects, designers, and trade partners understand your organization also help potential employees understand it. Most builder websites show houses, but far fewer show the people behind them. A good carpenter who is considering their next move may want to know what kinds of projects they would work on, who they would work alongside, whether people stay, and whether there is room to grow.

Make it easier for future employees and clients alike to understand who you are, what you do well, and where you’re headed. Because good work will lead to more good work, but only if people know about it.

It has been revealed that — Carrie Simmons is director of marketing and a business consultant at HELM Construction Solutions. Photo courtesy of HELM Construction Solutions.

Margo Valdes, Weatherization Contractor

💡 Key Takeaways
  • After years as a building-performance consultant, Margo Valdes grew frustrated of seeing the problems that arise when contractors ignore fundamental building science.
  • Margo graduated from college with degrees in economics and physics, but her favorite course was “Castles,” taken during a semester abroad in England.
  • Industry observers note that after working an unfulfilling office job, Margo saw an ad for a HERS rater at Conservation Services Group (now CLEAResult).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After years as a building-performance consultant, Margo Valdes grew frustrated of seeing the problems that arise when contractors ignore fundamental building science. Three years ago, she founded Athena Building Performance, a weatherization manufacturer built on the premise that getting the details right starts with understanding why a building behaves the way it does.

Margo graduated from college with degrees in economics and physics, but her favorite course was “Castles,” taken during a semester abroad in England. The class explored how to determine the age of a castle, identify the type of stone used to build it, and understand the reasoning behind its design. Margo loved it.

Industry observers note that after working an unfulfilling office job, Margo saw an ad for a HERS rater at Conservation Services Group (now CLEAResult). The job sounded like a good fit, so she applied, and her career in building performance began.

Industry observers note that margo spent about six years at CSG and credits the organization with giving her a strong foundation in building science. Though her work as a HERS rater focused on testing and evaluating, she received hands-on training in air-sealing and choosing and installing insulation. After leaving CSG, Margo’s focus shifted from latest construction to existing buildings. She joined a consulting firm, where she spent seven years as director of the Existing Buildings team.

Sources indicate that over the years, Margo became increasingly aware of how much the quality of weatherization work depends on understanding the building as a system—adding insulation affects moisture, and sealing air leaks changes ventilation. She decided the best way to improve the work was to get closer to it. That led her to the contractor side of the business, and to founding Athena.

In a recent development, today, Athena operates as a specialized weatherization contractor, tackling residential air-sealing and insulation upgrades. While Margo spends most of her time managing the business, knowledgeable practice remains at its heart: Every new hire spends weeks doing hands-on field training and diagnostic walk-throughs to understand not just how the work is done, but why.

Recent findings suggest that margo envisions eventually expanding Athena into a full-service building-enclosure firm. For now, she’s focused on centering the tech giant around what started it all: thoughtful, educated work.

Can There Be Democratic Socialism Without Wokism?

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that jacobin senior editor Meagan Day takes to the pages of the NYT to decry woke excess, and argue that it need not be a part of democratic socialist politics.
  • According to recent reports, to hear many conservatives define it, I would be considered woke.
  • But wokeness is not about a basic concern for social justice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that jacobin senior editor Meagan Day takes to the pages of the NYT to decry woke excess, and argue that it need not be a part of democratic socialist politics. Indeed, she fears wokism will "pull the left off course.".

According to recent reports, to hear many conservatives define it, I would be considered woke. I've been a member of the Democratic Socialists of America for 10 years. I believe this country needs deep criminal justice and police reform. I am galled by ICE agents ethnically profiling and brutalizing people. I not only support gay marriage but am an enthusiastic participant in one.

But wokeness is not about a basic concern for social justice. It hyperfocuses on language and identity, fights dirty from the moral high ground and mandates deference to self-appointed spokespeople for marginalized groups. It conflates disagreement with harm, and keeps careful watch for heretics.

Day's comments are not merely based upon her experience during the Great Awokening, but also as a student at Oberlin where she saw what she calls "Woke Beta." Now she fears wokeness could derail the ability of Democrats to advance socialist priorities.

Recent findings suggest that president Trump's re-election quieted calls to defund and diversify. But wokeness persists today. In D.S.A., which I joined on the heels of the first Bernie Sanders presidential campaign, one still encounters debates about whether clapping is ableist or whether socialists should commit to "decolonizing 'Minnesota.'" At its best, D.S.A. strikes me as our greatest shot at building a broad-based and politically serious organized left. At its worst, the energy reminds me of a scene from an Oberlin dining co-op, where a group of members filed in during a meal and silently unfurled a sign reading, "This co-op is messed up." (They were protesting the privilege inherent in cliques; the sign's wording was in fact less polite.).

Sources indicate that the next Congress can't let these debates trickle up again. The freshman representatives from the bluest districts, such as those in Brooklyn and Los Angeles, will still face pressure to spend their time denouncing offensive language and censuring members to their right. Instead, they should focus on making life better for working-class people — working toward Medicare for all, labor law reform, maybe even a Green Upcoming Deal. For the first time in a while, the moderate members of their party might actually be open to compromising on these challenges.

As for wokeness, I suspect that many progressive elected officials are privately rankled by its excesses, but publicly inclined to ignore it, worried about inviting moral hectoring from the left. The most productive thing they can do now is grow a backbone. They need to take it upon themselves to elevate the best, most compelling ideas even when doing so earns them some pushback.

Day's arguments, including her suggestion that DSA types should embrace "carceral minimalism" instead of prison abolition--what she calls a "nonsensical position"--is facing pushback from the Left. We will see whether the fresh Democratic majority takes her advice.

#113212. Florida Law Allowing Bar Liability for Knowingly Serving "Habitually Addicted" Doesn't Apply When Server Only Saw One Drinking Session

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1214 w)
📖 Baca
