Florida Law Allowing Bar Liability for Knowingly Serving "Habitually Addicted" Doesn't Apply When Server Only Saw One Drinking Session

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1214 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, from Croteau v.
  • It has been revealed that in this personal injury case, the plaintiff appeals from the circuit court's final summary judgment which found … that the plaintiff could not prove her negligence action against a bar which had served her alcoholic beverages before she was injured later that night.
  • According to recent reports, liability for injury or damage resulting from intoxication.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, from Croteau v. Family 5, Inc., decided Wednesday by Florida Court of Appeal Chief Judge Jonathan Gerber, joined by Judges Marlon Weiss and Johnathan Lott:.

It has been revealed that in this personal injury case, the plaintiff appeals from the circuit court's final summary judgment which found … that the plaintiff could not prove her negligence action against a bar which had served her alcoholic beverages before she was injured later that night. The summary judgment rested on the circuit court's application of "the dram shop statute"—section 768.125, Florida Statutes (2020):.

According to recent reports, liability for injury or damage resulting from intoxication. A person who sells or furnishes alcoholic beverages to a person of lawful drinking age shall not thereby become liable for injury or damage caused by or resulting from the intoxication of such person, except that a person who willfully and unlawfully sells or furnishes alcoholic beverages to a person who is not of lawful drinking age or who knowingly serves a person habitually addicted to the use of any or all alcoholic beverages may become liable for injury or damage caused by or resulting from the intoxication of such minor or person.

In a recent development, the underlined second exception is at concern here…. In addressing "what constitutes 'knowledge' in order for a vendor's conduct to be found negligent," the [Florida Supreme Court has] found:.

In a recent development, [T]he cause of action [under section 768.125's second exception] only requires evidence that the vendor had knowledge that the individual the vendor served was a habitual drunkard. Serving an individual multiple drinks on one occasion would be insufficient, in and of itself, to establish that the vendor knowingly served a habitual drunkard alcoholic beverages. On the other hand, serving an individual a substantial number of drinks on multiple occasions would be circumstantial evidence to be considered by the jury in determining whether the vendor knew that the person was a habitual drunkard….

[In another case,] we affirmed a summary judgment for the defendant bar, where the plaintiff patron was unknown to the bar's staff, was not a bar regular, and had purchased up to four drinks over two to three hours. We held that we could not impute notice of the patron's alcohol addiction to the bar when the patron had not shown any signs of intoxication, despite his alcohol consumption ….

Here, consistent with [those precedents], the bar's serving the alcoholic beverages to the plaintiff for the first time on the incident date, without more, should not be considered sufficient evidence to impute knowledge to the bar that the plaintiff was "habitually addicted to the use of any or all alcoholic beverages." ….

Roster v. Moulton (Fla. App. 1992)—the primary case upon which the plaintiff relies—is distinguishable….

According to recent reports, [In Roster,] [i]t is undisputed that [the patron] consumed 8–10, 12–ounce cans of beer and two straight shots of tequila over the period of an hour and a half. After a short absence from [the bar], during which [the patron] drank yet another beer served elsewhere, [the patron] returned to [the bar's] walk-up window, where he ordered and was served another beer. The [bar manager] admitted that it would be unusual for a person to consume that many beers and two shots of tequila without showing signs of intoxication. Despite [the patron's] considerable alcohol consumption, [the patron] did not stagger and did not slur his speech. The manager twice asked [the patron] to leave the bar only because [the patron] became loud and argumentative. [The patron] pled guilty to the charge of driving while under the influence of alcohol and admitted that he had a drinking problem from the age of sixteen, which he still had at the time of the accident. At that time, [the patron] had never received treatment for his alcohol addiction….

Industry observers note that by affidavit in Roster, "two experts[] … essentially stated that the large amount of alcohol that [the patron had] consumed over a relatively short time period, together with the lack of impairment [which the patron had] demonstrated, would have put a reasonable server of alcohol on notice that [the patron] was habitually addicted to alcohol. [The bar] submitted no affidavits to oppose these viewpoints." ….

However, unlike in Roster, as the bar's answer brief submits:.

It has been revealed that … [W]hatever alcohol [the plaintiff] may have consumed at [the bar], she claims she drank over a five-hour period—much longer than the 90 minutes during which the Roster [patron] consumed 10–12 drinks. Furthermore, [the plaintiff] claims she sat, ordered drink(s), and watched television for five hours, which is much different than the Roster [patron,] who left the bar …, drank another alcoholic beverage elsewhere, and then came back to the bar where he was served yet another drink. Also, unlike … in Roster, there is no evidence that [the plaintiff] demonstrated a level of intoxication consistent with someone who had either a high or low tolerance for alcohol. Finally, unlike the [patron] in Roster, [the plaintiff here] did not become loud or argumentative at the [bar]. By her own admission, she was quiet, not boisterous, not loud, not abusive, and she simply kept to herself….

Unlike the Roster patron, the plaintiff here was an anonymous patron, whose behavior during her visit to the bar was, by her own statements, unremarkable.

Judge Lott agreed, but added that he thought Roster was wrongly decided, including in its reliance on expert evidence:.

Section 768.125, Florida Statutes (2020), says that a bar owner is not liable for damage caused by the sale of alcoholic beverages, except that (as relevant here) a person "who knowingly serves a person habitually addicted to the use of any or all alcoholic beverages may become liable." The language does not require expert testimony, and does not ask how the latest version of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) defines pathologies related to alcohol use….

Sources indicate that the statutory language asks whether the server has actual knowledge that the person is, as a matter of habit, addicted to alcohol…. You know such a thing when you see it—and it's hard to imagine being able to see it given only a single occasion of indulgence…. [A]nyone can have too many drinks. What separates a "habitual drunkard" [which is how the concurrence elsewhere interprets "habitually addicted"] is that the habitual drunkard feels compelled to do so on account of their addiction, and does so regularly as a matter of habit….

Industry observers note that turning back to Roster—where was the evidence that the defendant actually knew that the plaintiff was habitually addicted to alcohol? The defendant observed the plaintiff drink heavily on one occasion wherein he handled his liquor well, until he didn't. No evidence of "addiction" was presented, much less of a "habit" of it. The expert affidavits about his apparent alcohol tolerance added nothing to that inquiry.

Industry observers note that in sum, Roster passed the buck from the statutory language to expert opinion, and reached the wrong result in turn. In an appropriate case, we should consider whether to recede from it….

Sources indicate that jack R. Reiter and Robert C. Weill (GrayRobinson, P.A.) represent the bar.

Dissolving Into the Forest

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This home was designed with two main goals in mind.
  • Outside, three irregular, offset buildings—the main house, a sauna, and a garden shed—mimic the tree-filled landscape, while Nakamoto Forestry’s Gendai yakisugi charred-wood siding provides a darkened exterior reminiscent of the texture of tree bark.
  • Inside, the dark, textured exterior gives way to bright, airy interiors filled with natural light, lighter wood finishes, and carefully framed views.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This home was designed with two main goals in mind. The first was for it to integrate into its forest setting, making it feel at home among the trees. The second was to capture forest views from a light-filled yet intimate interior. By focusing on these goals, the architects designed a home that feels less like an object in the forest than a place quietly woven into it.

Outside, three irregular, offset buildings—the main house, a sauna, and a garden shed—mimic the tree-filled landscape, while Nakamoto Forestry’s Gendai yakisugi charred-wood siding provides a darkened exterior reminiscent of the texture of tree bark.

Inside, the dark, textured exterior gives way to bright, airy interiors filled with natural light, lighter wood finishes, and carefully framed views. Because the living spaces are stacked to fill the irregular form of the main house, each room provides a unique view of the landscape, with windows that vary in scale.

Large windows in the living room and a sliding glass door in the dining area allow in sunlight and views from different directions, the primary bedroom on the top floor includes a small north-facing window, and a large window next to the bathtub frames the view of an eastern hilltop.

The design team used the height of the ceilings to guide the function of each space, with cathedral ceilings creating a spacious effect in the main living spaces, cozier sloped ceilings in the primary bedroom and bathroom, and a welcoming reading nook in the second-floor bedroom where the roof slope drops to a low kneewall.

#113210. Breaking: Has Congress Learned How To Conduct Effective Oversight?

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (853 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Has Congress Learned How To Conduct Effective Oversight?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (853 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that democratic leaders have promised that their new congressional majorities will focus on affordability and accountability.
  • Listening to some talk about their plans, such as in this Ezra Klein interview with incoming House Oversight Chair Robert Garcia, I wonder whether House Democrats have learned that Congress's oversight and investigation authority is not as all-encompassing as some might think.
  • In a recent development, I discuss the legal contours of Congressional oversight and investigatory authority in my latest Civitas Outlook column.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that democratic leaders have promised that their new congressional majorities will focus on affordability and accountability. They have also pledged to engage in extensive oversight and investigation of the Trump Administration, and firms and individuals that have operated within the White House's orbit.

Listening to some talk about their plans, such as in this Ezra Klein interview with incoming House Oversight Chair Robert Garcia, I wonder whether House Democrats have learned that Congress's oversight and investigation authority is not as all-encompassing as some might think. The authority to conduct inquiries for legislative purposes is broad, but it has limits. And during the first Trump Administration, the failure of House Democrats to contend with those limits hampered oversight efforts.

In a recent development, I discuss the legal contours of Congressional oversight and investigatory authority in my latest Civitas Outlook column. In this piece, I explain why Trump v. Mazars is the greater constraint on free-wheeling fishing expeditions than is the Trump immunity decision.

Nothing in the Constitution expressly grants Congress the power to investigate executive branch agencies, let alone the President (or anyone else, for that matter). The authority to conduct oversight is an adjunct to Congress's legislative powers. In the simplest terms, it is often necessary and proper for Congress to secure information and conduct inquiries as it considers legislation and makes appropriation decisions. Or, as the Court explained in Mazars, this "power of inquiry—with process to enforce it—is an essential and appropriate auxiliary to the legislative function." , , ,.

According to recent reports, no justice in Mazars endorsed the then-common view that Congress could demand all information it sought, subject only to the constraints imposed by Executive Privilege. Rather, the justices were unanimous that Congress lacks the power to investigate for investigation's sake, or to conduct oversight for the purpose of public disclosure or inducing prosecution. Congress has no authority to try private citizens in a committee hearing. As the Chief Justice explained in his opinion for the Court, congressional subpoenas are valid only insofar as they are "related to, and in furtherance of, a legitimate task of the Congress." More generally, congressional subpoenas must serve "a valid legislative purpose," and Congress bears the burden of demonstrating this standard is met. Document demands that appear designed more to harass or punish the political opposition than to inform legitimate legislative activity will not be enforced.

Industry observers note that insofar as Congress wishes to investigate the White House or high-ranking officials, its greatest investigatory authority is not the power to inquire for legislative purposes. Rather, it is the power to impeach. In practice, this means some of the greater restraints on Congressional oversight are political, rather than legal.

Recent findings suggest that while the Court's decision in Mazars focused on the connection between document demands and the legislative process, this is not the only path Congress may take. The Constitution grants Congress the power to enact legislation for various purposes. It also delegates the power to impeach, and these powers are distinct. As Judge Neomi Rao explained when the Mazars case was before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, "investigations of impeachable offenses simply are not, and never have been, within Congress's legislative power." They stand on their own bottom.

Recent findings suggest that this distinction matters, because if Congress wishes to investigate potentially impeachable offenses, it must be clear that is what it is doing so voters can evaluate its actions accordingly. "Allowing Congress to investigate impeachable officials for suspicions of criminality pursuant to the legislative power has serious consequences for the separation of powers because it allows Congress to escape the responsibility and accountability inherent in impeachment proceedings," Judge Rao warned. This wolf must come as a wolf.

According to recent reports, and on Trump v. U.S., I take a different view than some other legal commentators:.

Industry observers note that some commentators fear that the Supreme Court's presidential immunity decision in Trump v. United States will hamper otherwise legitimate congressional inquiries. "Congress cannot act on, and courts cannot examine, the President's actions on subjects within his 'conclusive and preclusive' constitutional authority," the Court declared. While this insulates the President from criminal prosecution for actions within the core of executive authority and would accordingly limit the Congress' ability to subpoena related information for legislative oversight purposes, it is no shield in matters of impeachment.

Aggressive Congressional oversight of the executive branch is not upcoming. Nor is the politicization of oversight. Once political parties emerged, it was inevitable that party loyalty would rival (if not overcome) each branch's institutional imperatives. Oversight fights were once more political than legal, but Congress could also defend its prerogatives without invoking the courts. A Congress that legislates and appropriates through regular order has more weapons to deploy and a greater ability to force executive branch acquiescence. Insofar as the next round of oversight fights are resolved in court, it will be yet another sign of Congress's decline.

For a deeper dive, my Cato Supreme Court Review article on the Mazars and Vance decisions is here.

The owners of this 1940s house wanted to add more space for a growing family, but site restrictions would only allow them to build upward, meaning the small home would tower over surrounding houses. To preserve the house’s place in the neighborhood and keep costs down, the solution was to remodel the existing space with a more functional layout, transforming the second floor from two bedrooms and one bath into three bedrooms and two baths while making the home feel more spacious, flexible, and connected.

It has been revealed that outside, the remodeled house maintains the same proportions of the original but incorporates modern updates such as the ACRE composite-wood entry accents and the single entry-door sidelight. To improve flow inside, the main staircase was relocated to create a more functional, open interior. Newly introduced sliding glass doors offer more light inside and a seamless connection to the outdoors, maximizing the feeling of space. The basement stairs are now accessed via a hidden floor hatch, preserving the open main living area.

Creating a more functional home within the same footprint means making the most of every inch of usable space. The area under the main staircase now houses deep storage drawers, and a new window seat offers extra space next to the picture window.

Industry observers note that on the exterior, the window-seat bump-out lets the house live larger without increasing its footprint. Clad in the same wood as the front entry, the bump-out creates a cohesive and striking connection between the front and back of the house.

A common theme in home design is the idea of blending the architecture with the landscape, allowing the building to sit lightly on the land. You might not expect a 4350-sq.-ft. modern home to be a shining example of how to achieve that goal, but this upcoming modern home in Bend, Ore., balances a striking architectural presence with a remarkably light touch on the landscape below.

The newly introduced building required enough space to house multiple generations, but maximum exposure to the meadow setting and mountain views meant siting the house on a hilltop. To meet both requirements while also only lightly interrupting the land, 40% of the home is set above grade, with a cantilevered great room that appears to float over the ground and that is supported by two special-ordered structural steel beams.

To further capitalize on the views, the common spaces feature expansive glazing, including a 40-ft. sliding glass wall, while roof overhangs allow the exterior to become part of the interior when large doors are open—while also providing shade and protection from the elements.

Recent findings suggest that because the house might accommodate one or two people at some times and upwards of 10 at others, the floor strategy is broken up into both large and small common spaces. These include a great room centered around a concrete fireplace designed for larger groups, and a roof deck for more intimate gatherings.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In this video, Andrew LeGrand of LeGrand Tiling Organization walks through a full backsplash installation, sharing his product recommendations and pro tips along the way. From prepping the work area, laying out the tile, and mixing and applying thinset, to cutting and installing the tile, grouting the tile, cleaning the tile surface, and sealing the tile, you’ll learn how to get quality results every time. Whether you’re tackling your first tile project or want to tighten up your technique, this video shows exactly how a pro gets it done.

It has been revealed that hey guys, this is Andrew LeGrand with LeGrand Tiling. We’re in Upstate Newly introduced York and we’re working on a backsplash here. In preparation we took off all the switch plates and all the outlet plates.

Although drywall is a good substrate to install tile to, behind wet areas I do like to add waterproof board, and between the countertop and the waterproof board I’ll do a bead of silicone just to ensure some waterproofing back there. So we’re using a 3×6 tile. We’re going to do very minimal spacing, and we’re going to do a subway pattern throughout this backsplash.

With these ceramic tiles what I’ll do is I’ll soak them for a couple minutes. What that does is introduces water to the ceramic, and it gives me a better bond with my thinset. Now these tiles have been soaking for a couple minutes. We’re going to pull them out and let them dry for a little bit before we install them.

Sources indicate that on my backsplashes, I like to use MULTIMAX™ Lite. It’s a premium thinset. When I’m mixing, I like to add water to my bucket and then add the thinset that is desired, and I start mixing.

Recent findings suggest that I’m looking for kind of a frosty peanut butter, toothpaste-type consistency. After I mix it for one minute and have the consistency that I like, then I let it slake for five minutes, and then I whip it back up before using it to install.

I’m going to use a drywall knife to first add the mud to the drywall, and then I’ll be able to come through with my notch trowel and add the notches. I’ll take my drywall knife here or my margin trowel and I’ll just back-butter the tile. I’ll adhere it to the wall, and I’ll give it a little bit of a wiggle just to collapse those ridges.

It has been revealed that and that is the kind of the coverage we want. Overall that’s pretty good coverage. As you can see, I am installing the tile directly to the countertop. There is a slight natural edge to this tile, and that’ll give it some space so sealant can grab in there.

Sources indicate that now that we have our first row installed, we’re doing a brick pattern, so I’m going to measure my tile. It’s about 5-1/16. So what I’ll do is go 2-1/2 and just a hair over 2-1/2 right there, and then I’ll put this tile on my score and snap, lining it up with the centerline, snap it, and then take this piece, put this on the inside there.

When it comes to doing outlets, I typically like to set my tile tight up against the one to the right and line up so the outlet is where it needs to be.

I will make a mark over here at the end of this outlet box and a mark over here, and then I’ll take my tile, set it on top of there, and I will make a mark just about here, trying not to cover up where the screw mounts to the box.

Now that we’ve finished this section of the backsplash, we’re going to add a metal trim piece along the wall here to bridge the tile and the drywall. I’m going to take some thinset on my drywall knife, and I’m just going to push thinset into those voids to adhere it to the wall. We’re going to add a little bit more thinset to the wall. We’ll come through with our notch trowel and add our notches to the wall.

Now that I’ve finished up this backsplash here, we’re going to roll on to installing this wall into our lower section and our wet wall and start installing tile there. So we’ve finished installing our tile. We’re now going to mix up a little bit of grout, just about half the bag.

We’re going to add a little bit of water. And then I prefer to mix by hand. We want to mix our grout for a couple minutes until we have a smooth consistency, and then we’ll let it sit for five minutes and come back and stir it back up. To grout, I’m going to take my grout float, get it in the bucket, just get a little bit on it, and just push that grout right into the grout joints.

Now that we’ve given our grout about 30 minutes to set up, we’re going to take a clean sponge and a clean bucket of water and we’re going to wipe down our grout.

Now that we’re done wiping with our sponge and getting the majority of the grout off the surface of our tile, we’re going to give it about 10 minutes. We’ll come back through with a damp microfiber and wipe off any excess and smooth out the grout joints.

According to recent reports, now that our grout is cured, we’re going to seal our grout. First, we’re going to wipe down with a dry microfiber to remove any excess dust or debris, and then we’ll come through, put the sealer on this microfiber, and apply it to our grout surface.

It has been revealed that now that we’ve applied the sealer, we’re going to let it sit for about 10 or 15 minutes. We’ll come through with a dry rag and wipe off all the excess sealer.

Now that we’ve sealed our tile, we’re going to move on to the final step. We’re going to use 100% silicone in between where our tile meets our countertop, where our tile meets in the inside corner, and where our tile meets the bottom of the cabinets.

It has been revealed that one thing I like while installing silicone is wearing a pair of gloves, so that as you run your finger and tool that silicone, it doesn’t get on your skin and contaminate the silicone. Another thing I like is doing my best to keep the tip of my silicone as clean as possible while I’m running my bead.

Recent findings suggest that the backsplash is done. We’ve got our outlet and switch covers on. We’re going to remove our site protection and clean up.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From Judge Justin Olson (S.D. Ind.) Friday in Robinson-Cooper v. Ivy Tech South Bend-Elkhart:.

Plaintiff's response brief was initially due October 2, 2026. Dkt. 99. She received two extensions, pushing back her response deadline to November 16. Dkts. 91, 100. Plaintiff argues she has met the standard of excusable neglect because presenting all the evidence in her response, including evidence of five comparators in this employment-law case, "took more time than counsel had anticipated." Dkt. 105 at 2. The Court finds Plaintiff has shown excusable neglect, including because her filing was less than an hour late and because Defendants do not claim to be prejudiced by it, dkt. 107, and so GRANTS the motion at docket entry [105] and accepts docket entry 103 as timely filed.

Industry observers note that A court will often cut you slack for filing a day late (especially if it's just an hour late), unless the requirement is jurisdictional and thus not waivable. But no slack here as to the page limit, and because of the denial of leave to file a longer brief, "The Court will not consider any arguments Plaintiff makes after page 30 of her briefing." This means that plaintiff's arguments related to her Family Medical Leave Act claims are basically being forfeited, though her race and sex discrimination arguments are preserved. The court's reasoning:.

The Court's practices and procedures state:.

Industry observers note that if a party files a motion to extend the page limit at the same time the party's brief is due, the extension request will be denied absent a compelling and unanticipated reason for violating this rule. The Court will also not consider any arguments made in pages which exceed the Local Rules' requirements.

Plaintiff acknowledges this requirement. She states her oversized filing, "results from counsel's underestimate of the space and time needed to present the comparator evidence, and the space needed to reference each cite pursuant to the docket number." As Defendants point out, Plaintiff has not provided a "compelling and unanticipated" reason for her oversized brief. The Court accordingly DENIES her motion to file an oversize response.

National Security Division Introduces First “Near Miss” Non-Prosecution Agreement Under the Department-wide Corporate Enforcement Policy

📅 27 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (789 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fbi

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the Department of Justice revealed today that it has entered into a non-prosecution agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc.
  • The Department reached the agreement under its 2026 Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy (“the Policy”), which incentivizes companies to voluntarily disclose discovered misconduct, cooperate with Department investigations, and timely and appropriately remediate the wrongdoing.
  • Sources indicate that this agreement with Extreme Networks marks the Department’s first non-prosecution agreement in a “near-miss” case under the Policy, meaning a case that involved full cooperation and appropriate remediation but did not qualify for a declination of prosecution.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the Department of Justice revealed today that it has entered into a non-prosecution agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc. The manufacturer agreed to pay criminal penalties totaling $975,721.84 to resolve the Department’s investigation of sanctions and export control offenses.

The Department reached the agreement under its 2026 Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy (“the Policy”), which incentivizes companies to voluntarily disclose discovered misconduct, cooperate with Department investigations, and timely and appropriately remediate the wrongdoing.

Sources indicate that this agreement with Extreme Networks marks the Department’s first non-prosecution agreement in a “near-miss” case under the Policy, meaning a case that involved full cooperation and appropriate remediation but did not qualify for a declination of prosecution. While Extreme Networks’ disclosure to the National Security Division (NSD) was not timely because it occurred under imminent threat of disclosure by a news publication, Extreme Networks nonetheless fully cooperated with the Department’s investigation and timely and appropriately remediated the misconduct. As a result, its disclosure qualified as a “Near Miss” Voluntary Self-Disclosure under the Policy.

It has been revealed that “This non-prosecution agreement and million-dollar criminal penalty mark the successful resolution of our investigation into the illegal sale of advanced networking equipment and services to a Russian weapons manufacturer, in clear violation of U.S. sanctions and export controls,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “The FBI remains dedicated to keeping sensitive technology out of the hands of the Russian military, and we're grateful to Homeland Security Investigations and the Bureau of Industry and Security for their partnership on this case. Let this announcement serve as a clear warning: if you attempt to arm our adversaries by violating U.S. law, justice will find you.”.

In a recent development, “HSI remains committed to investigating companies and individuals who evade U.S. export controls and sanctions to provide goods or services to foreign weapons manufacturers,” remarked Acting Special Agent in Charge Jeremy Pierczynski of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Detroit. “These laws protect our national security and prevent U.S.-origin products and services from supporting adversaries’ military capabilities. HSI will continue working with our law enforcement and regulatory partners to identify and hold accountable those who undermine these critical safeguards.”.

The agreement arose out of an investigation into Extreme Networks’ sales of products and services to Moscow Machinery Building Plant Avangard (MMZA), a Russian weapons manufacturer that was owned by JSC Concern Almaz-Antey (Almaz Antey), which was added to the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List by the Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in July 2014.

Pursuant to the non-prosecution agreement, Extreme Networks will forfeit $487,860.92 in proceeds from the sanctions and export control offenses and pay a criminal fine of $487,860.92, for a total criminal penalty of $975,721.84. Extreme Networks will also resolve a parallel administrative action by OFAC.

Industry observers note that between around March 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks, through its then-Russia based subsidiary, Extreme Networks Rus LLC, processed and fulfilled 11 purchase orders for networking equipment and services to MMZA without the required license or authorization from OFAC. MMZA was a primary producer of the S-300 and S-400 anti-aircraft missile systems used by the Russian army. To facilitate these sales, certain Russia-based Extreme Networks employees concealed the identity of MMZA from Extreme Networks’ global trade compliance group, causing Extreme Networks to file false electronic export information via the Automated Export System and smuggle goods from the United States. Through this scheme, Extreme Networks deprived the U.S. government of its ability to carry out its lawful function of enforcing sanctions and export controls designed to protect national security and economic interests. As a result of its unlawful conduct, Extreme Networks earned approximately $487,860.92 in revenue from the sales of goods and services.

In a recent development, although Extreme Networks’ self-disclosure to NSD was not timely pursuant to the Policy, Extreme Networks nonetheless cooperated with the Department’s investigation by timely providing relevant facts and documents and making employees available for interviews. Extreme Networks also appropriately remediated the misconduct by terminating its contract with the third-party distributor it used to facilitate these sales, improving screening procedures, hiring additional compliance personnel, and implementing diligence procedures in connection with mergers and acquisitions. Given these steps and the lack of aggravating circumstances, the Department agreed to enter into a non-prosecution agreement.

The FBI Charlotte Field Office, the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security, and Homeland Security Investigations investigated the case.

This case was prosecuted by former Trial Attorney Maria Fedor of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Adam Hulbig for the Eastern District of North Carolina.

Please see the Justice Department’s policy here.

Near that same time, White texted photographs to Sarah of the two of them having sex…. [T]he State charged White with two counts of breach of privacy for White unlawfully disseminating the illicit video and photographs to Sarah ….

The breach of privacy statute provides:.

"(a) Breach of privacy is knowingly and without lawful authority: …. (8) disseminating any videotape, photograph, film or image of another identifiable person 18 years of age or older who is nude or engaged in sexual activity and under circumstances in which such identifiable person had a reasonable expectation of privacy, with the intent to harass, threaten or intimidate such identifiable person, and such identifiable person did not consent to such dissemination." ….

The court held White didn't violate the statute:.

Here Sarah consented to the photos being taken and the video being made. White later emailed and texted the sexually explicit material only to Sarah. How did that conduct breach Sarah's privacy? ….

In a recent development, sarah had an expectation of privacy as to the photos and the video to the extent that she could reasonably expect that no one other than she and White would ever see the sexually explicit images. White did not violate that expectation of privacy.

Recent findings suggest that the evidence showed that White transmitted the sexually explicit material to Sarah with the intent to harass her. But for there to be a breach of privacy under [the statute], the term "disseminating" requires that the illicit material be sent to someone other than the person depicted in the material and who consented to the illicit material being made. White's conduct here more than likely constituted harassment by telecommunication device in violation of K.S.A. 21-6206, but we find it did not constitute breach of privacy….

It has been revealed that if the outlets in a room aren’t where you need them and you’ve got extension cords running amok, adding an outlet can eliminate those trip hazards and make everyday living a bit easier. Or maybe you need a upcoming outlet in a bathroom, laundry room, or doggy wash station in your mudroom, which means you’ll need to install a ground fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) outlet, required for any outlet within 6 feet of a water source. The good news is, wiring an outlet, whether standard or GFCI, is a project that you can do yourself, but you must take proper safety precautions.

However, if an outlet’s cover has melted, if the outlet has been smoking, or if there’s a burning smell, there’s likely a bigger matter than just the outlet. In these instances, it’s best to consult with a licensed electrician before you attempt to rewire it.

Read through these steps for how to wire an outlet before you get started.

Industry observers note that while a capable homeowner can wire an outlet, it’s not a job for a reluctant or unsure DIYer. Start by assessing your comfort level, and call in a pro if you have doubts.

In many instances, you can wire an outlet from another outlet. In fact, if there’s an existing outlet in a room on the opposite side of the wall from where you’d like to add an outlet, the job can be pretty simple. In this situation, you can usually cut a new opening, install an electrical box, and add a new outlet without having to snake wires through studs. Use a stud finder to locate the studs on either side of the existing outlet and make sure to situate the new outlet within the same stud bay.

It has been revealed that if you simply want more outlets in one location, it’s possible to replace an existing duplex outlet, which takes just two plugs, with a quad receptacle, which takes four. This can be helpful in a workshop or even in kitchens and bathrooms where two outlets just won’t cut it.

In either case, it’s important that there’s enough capacity on the circuit to accommodate the additional draw. For 15-amp circuits, the maximum is usually eight outlets or lights. Any more receptacles than that might draw too much current for the breaker.

Old-fashioned two-prong outlet connections aren’t grounded, which makes them dangerous in the event of an electrical fault. Without an electrician, it’s safe to convert a two-prong to a three-prong outlet only if the electrical box housing the outlet is metal and the cable feeding the box is armored. If these conditions are met, the box provides ground-fault protection (even though the outlet does not).

According to recent reports, how can you tell, without opening the wall, if the electrical box meets the criteria? Simple: Use a voltage tester. Insert one prong into the outlet’s shorter slot (the “hot slot”), then touch the other prong to the screw securing the faceplate. If the tester lights up, the electrical box is grounded, and you can go ahead and convert the two-prong to a three-prong. If your electrical box isn’t grounded, you can still convert to a three-prong, but the replacement must be a GFCI (the type of outlet with a red button on its front).

Over time, electrical outlets can start to look dingy or dirty, or the plastic can crack and make the outlet dangerous to use. To keep power flowing where you need it, it’s important to learn how to replace an electrical outlet safely and efficiently.

4-in-1 screwdriverVoltage testerOutlet.

Before you go any further, it’s imperative that you cut power to the outlet you are replacing. At your home’s electrical panel, toggle off the switch associated with the circuit that sends electricity to the outlet in question.

Recent findings suggest that after you shut off the power to the outlet, use a voltage tester to double-check that it’s really off. Insert the tester’s probes into the top two slots on the outlet. If the tester lights up, you toggled the wrong switch on the electrical panel and you’ll have to try again. Continue by trial and error until you are certain the outlet is no longer receiving electricity. (When you’re done, relabel the circuits in the panel so you know which is which.).

Industry observers note that don’t have a voltage tester? You can use a lamp instead, so long as you know the lamp works. Plug the lamp into the outlet, and if it doesn’t turn on, it’s safe to proceed. This method is inherently riskier, so use it only as a last resort.

After you confirm that the power is off to the outlet, stick a piece of black electrical tape across the breaker so no one can flip it back on while you are working.

It has been revealed that most faceplates have a single screw in the middle. Remove that screw, and the plate should come off easily. Next, unscrew the mounting screws that secure the outlet to the electrical box. Finally, gently pull the outlet away from the receptacle.

You can now see three wires extending from the wall to the outlet. If the wires are attached to screws on the outlet, loosen those screws to free the wires. If the wires are snaked into holes in the back of the outlet, press the release slot and pull the wires out, assuming they don’t come out on their own. Put aside the old outlet.

You’re now ready to wire in the replacement. First, connect the neutral wire (white) to the silver screw on the side of the outlet. Make sure to orient the hooked end of the wire so that its curve goes clockwise, the same direction in which you will tighten the screw.

Connect the ground wire to the green screw, using the technique described above.

Connect the hot wire (black) to the gold screw, the last one remaining on the outlet casing.

Recent findings suggest that carefully maneuver the wires back into the electrical box, then screw the outlet to the box using the mounting screws at the top and bottom. Finally, position the faceplate over the outlet and screw it back on.

Go back to the electrical panel and restore power to the outlet that you’ve finished replacing. Check the outlet installation by testing the device with a voltage tester or a lamp.

Sometimes a simple replacement isn’t enough—you absolutely need another outlet. Maybe you want to accommodate a fresh appliance or entertainment device, or you’re setting up a workshop. You can frequently solve this problem by wiring a new outlet from an existing outlet on the other side of the wall from the desired location of the new outlet. This project is a bit more involved, but a safety-minded DIYer can take it on.

In a recent development, note: Be sure you’re using an “old work,” “rework,” or “remodeling” electrical box for the new outlet. These boxes have tabs that squeeze the box against the back of the drywall to hold it in place.

Be sure to shut off the power to the existing outlet before doing anything else. Check the outlet for power with the voltage tester, and then go to the electrical panel to shut off the corresponding breaker.

It has been revealed that head back to the outlet and use a voltage tester to ensure that the power is off. Once you confirm that the power is off, it’s a good idea to place a piece of black electrical tape across the breaker to prevent anyone from carelessly flipping it back on.

According to recent reports, place the electrical box face-first against the drywall where you blueprint to install it. Trace along the box’s edges with a pencil, and then cut along the marks with a drywall saw. Sometimes it’s easier if you score the drywall with a utility knife first.

Recent findings suggest that head back to the existing outlet. If it’s been some time since you shut the breaker, test the outlet again to make sure it’s still off. Next, remove the faceplate and remove the screws holding the outlet in the box. Carefully pull the outlet out and let it hang to one side, providing access to the back of the box.

According to recent reports, push the upcoming wire through an opening in the back of the box, feeding enough wire into the wall to reach the new outlet opening plus 1 foot. This can be challenging, so be patient and use pliers to pull the tab open if necessary. On this same side, cut the new wire approximately 10 inches from the box. Carefully strip back the plastic sheathing, leaving approximately 1 inch of sheathing in the box.

Use the screwdriver to loosen the screws holding the existing wires onto the outlet and straighten the hooks with needle-nose pliers. Use wire strippers to remove approximately ⅝ inch of sheathing from the hot (black) wire and neutral (white) wire.

Still working with the existing outlet, cut a 6- to 7-inch length from the spool of electrical cable. Remove the white, black, and ground wires from within the sheathing, and strip the ends back approximately ⅝ inch. This wire is called a pigtail.

Use the lineman pliers to twist the ends of the existing wire, the new wire, and one end of the pigtail into a clockwise twist. Do this in three sets: all black wires, all white wires, and all ground wires. Cap each twist with a wire connector.

In a recent development, use the needle-nose pliers to bend the wires at the other end of the pigtail into a J-shape and hook them onto the outlet. White (neutral) goes to silver, black (hot) goes to gold, and ground goes to green. Be sure that the hooks are running clockwise before tightening the screws.

Head to the other side of the wall to the space you’ve cut out for the new outlet. If the new wire isn’t easy to find, use a fishhook or tape from a wire running kit to fish it out from the wall. Pull the electric outlet wiring through the new opening, and feed the end into the new remodeling box.

Fit the box into the opening and turn the screws attached to the tabs clockwise until the box is secure. You should have about 10 inches of upcoming wire coming through the box. Strip the plastic sheathing back to expose the hot, neutral, and ground wires, leaving approximately 1 inch of sheathed cable inside the box.

Industry observers note that use the wire stripper to strip the sheathing from the ends of the hot, neutral, and ground wires, exposing approximately ⅝ inch of bare wire. Use the needle-nose pliers to bend the ends of the wires into hooks, and slip them over the screws on the upcoming outlet. Remember to follow typical receptacle wiring techniques: Connect the white wire to the silver screw, the black wire to the gold screw, and the bare copper wire to the ground screw. Finally, bend the wires so they will fold nicely as you attach the outlet to the box.

Tighten the screws at the top and bottom of the outlet until it is snug in the box. Put the faceplate on the outlet and tighten the screw. Flip the breaker back on and test the outlet.

In a recent development, learning how to wire an electrical outlet isn’t overwhelmingly difficult, and it’s a skill that some DIYers will use time and time again. With a little bit of background and proper safety techniques, adding an outlet for a TV or a latest tool or appliance can be a breeze. Just remember to work safely, test and retest electrical outlets before you start, and follow the instructions above for a reliable and safe electrical outlet installation.

There are many types of electrical wires, and to explain them all would require an electrical engineering textbook. The most common residential wiring, including standard electrical outlet wiring colors, involves three types.

It has been revealed that you absolutely can wire a light switch to an outlet, and there are several ways to do so. The switch can either be installed between the source of the power (typically the panel) and the outlet, or on a loop after the outlet.

To install it in-line, simply run the wire through an electrical box, connect the hot wire to the switch so it can interrupt the flow of power, and then continue the hot wire out to the outlet and wire as normal.

Industry observers note that to install the light switch after the device, connect the neutral wire in the box as usual, then run a length of wire from the outlet to the switch. Connect one end of the wire to the existing hot wire in the box using wire connectors. Next, connect the black wire from this length to one side of the switch, and connect the white wire to the other side. Finally, head back to the outlet and connect the white wire to the gold screw and wrap black electrical tape around the wire to indicate that it is now the hot lead coming from a switch.

The easiest way to fix an outlet that does not have a proper ground wire is to replace it with a GFCI outlet. These devices detect ground faults and interrupt the circuit right away. Install a GFCI in place of the first power outlet in the run to offer grounding protection.

Of course, contact a local electrical inspector to ensure this meets local codes.

Whether you’re part of the growing gig economy and looking to soundproof your home office, your teen has rock star dreams, or your 8-year-old has started tap-dancing, you’ll find that a little soundproofing can go a long way toward keeping the peace and quiet at home.

Room soundproofing techniques will reduce sound transfer from one room to another, but they won’t eliminate the loudest noises. These techniques can be used for any type of room—a home office, a nursery, or a family room, or to create a soundproof bedroom.

Mass-loaded vinyl (MLV) is a sound-dampening product used everywhere from nightclubs and recording studios to hockey rinks, and it’s among the best soundproofing materials available. It comes on a roll and costs around $2 per square foot, depending on weight, length, and width. The thicker it is, the better it will be for blocking noise and ending echoes, but thickness, which can range from 1/16 inch to 1/4 inch, may not be listed in product specifications. It may instead be labeled by weight. Half-pound MLV weighs 1/2 pound per square foot of coverage and is 1/16 inch thick; 1-pound MLV is 1 pound per square foot of coverage and is 1/8 inch thick; 2-pound MLV is 1/4 inch thick.

Recent findings suggest that while MLV can be hung directly on a wall, it performs best when sandwiched between drywall sheets. Doing so also allows you aesthetic options since the usually black, shiny MLV isn’t the most decoratively appealing surface. Keep in mind that MLV, such as Soundsulate, is heavy and awkward to work with. Hanging it is a two-person job, so be sure to enlist a helper.

Prior to ordering MLV, carefully measure the walls you want to soundproof. Leaving gaps in MLV will drastically compromise its effectiveness, so you’ll want to buy enough for complete coverage from wall to wall and floor to ceiling. When calculating your needs, note that MLV tends to be sold on rolls of 2-foot or 4-foot widths.

Measure a length of MLV that will reach floor to ceiling and then cut out a sheet with the scissors or utility knife. Cutting on top of scrap wood would be wise to protect your floor or work surface.

Position the step ladder and put the MLV against the wall starting at either end, working to the other corner. To install it, snug it up against the ceiling, with your helper holding it in place. Using drywall nails and a hammer, attach the MLV to the upper portion of the wall at 12-inch intervals. Then attach the bottom portion at 12-inch intervals, and finally at 12- to 24-inch intervals down the sides of the sheet.

Repeat Steps 2 and 3 as required until the entire wall is covered. For the best soundproof wall, butt the MLV right up against the preceding sheet so there are no gaps. You can overlap it for a potentially greater sound barrier, but you’ll have bumps and ridges if you do so. Overlapping is not recommended if you strategy to paint, install wallpaper, or install additional drywall panels.

Hang drywall on top of the MLV to make the soundproofing twice as effective and give you a surface for paint or other wall covering decor. Or read on for a quick solution to hiding the glossy black vinyl with curtains—a no-commitment decor project that will also enhance soundproofing. Sometimes called “soundproof drywall,” Type X drywall is 5/8 inch thick and fire rated, making it among the best options for noise dampening.

Not for windows only, curtains can create drama on the walls of any room while offering considerable soundproofing benefits. They’re relatively inexpensive and as easy to remove as they are to install. While there are curtains specifically marketed as sound dampening or “acoustic,” blackout and thermal curtains, which are primarily sold to keep light out and warmth in, also provide noise reduction. Don’t let the term “blackout” fool you, though. These curtains come in many colors and styles—it’s the inner liner that provides the blackout/thermal effect. Even heavy fabrics like velvet provide some soundproofing.

In a recent development, keep in mind that when you double the weight of the fabric, its sound-reduction ability nearly triples. Yet more important than weight is curtain construction; pleated curtains can be three times as effective against noise as those that hang straight. The pleats double the fabric’s thickness in many areas and act as baffles, absorbing sound waves and stopping them in the fabric folds.

Sources indicate that remember, sound dampening is the goal, so floor-to-ceiling curtains covering the entire wall will have the most impact. For the best results, hang multiple panels of soundproof curtains to fill the wall. Good options include the BGment Blackout Curtains and Nicetown’s 100% Blackout Curtains. If you’re feeling adventurous, mix colors and patterns for a funky feature wall!

The Pony Dance Blackout Insulated Soundproof Curtains reduced sound by 10 decibels during our hands-on testing. See our full review.

Tape measureSound-absorbing curtains (preferably floor-to-ceiling length)Bathroom scaleHanging system for curtains (rods, wires, or other systems rated for your curtain weight)ScrewdriverScrewsStud finder (optional)Weight-rated drywall anchors (optional)Iron or Steamer.

It has been revealed that measure the walls before purchasing the curtains. When shopping, check package info for the curtains’ weight; you’ll need this to choose rods or another hanging system sturdy enough to hold them. If you’re set on curtains that don’t include the weight on the packaging, weigh them on your bathroom scale at home. Tip: Keep them in the package so they’ll sit easily on the scale.

According to recent reports, purchase a hanging system weight-rated for the curtains (packaging or website marketing should tell you the weight load they can handle). If they weigh 40 pounds and the wall to be covered is 12 feet long, you’ll need a rod or hanging system that can handle roughly 3.5 pounds per foot, so keep that weight rating in mind when making your choice. Heavy-duty, ceiling-mount brackets, such as the KXLIFE brackets, will hold the heaviest curtains.

Locate wall studs with a stud finder, or use proper weight-rated wall anchors before boring into the wall with screws. Affix the rod or hanging system to the walls as recommended by the manufacturer.

In a recent development, iron or steam curtains to remove creases and wrinkles from the packaging. Check the label to see what temperature the manufacturer suggests and iron accordingly.

According to recent reports, hang the curtains on the rod or wire system and then “bunch” them together in equal amounts across the entire wall for a consistent look. When soundproofing a room, keep in mind that pleated, bunched fabric will absorb more sound than flat fabric, so ample curtains are a plus.

Recent findings suggest that soundproofing a room’s walls will go a long way toward reducing unwanted noise, but for an even quieter room, consider soundproofing other areas. Depending on the type of noise and where it’s coming from, you may also want to add noise-dampening materials to windows, doors, and other areas in the room.

Recent findings suggest that windows let in fresh air and light, but if the window faces a busy urban street, the hustle and bustle of commuters, barking dogs, and emergency vehicles can make it seem as though they’re right in the room. To soundproof a room and mute noise transfer through windows, consider hanging one or more layers of thick curtains over windows, installing storm windows, or using a soundproof weather strip product, such as a draft stopper, to block noise. Soundproofing windows is a vital step in reducing unwanted noise.

Sources indicate that interior doors often have a gap at the bottom that allows air (and noise) to enter a room. Soundproofing a door typically involves using a product that will seal the gap. To soundproof a bedroom door or home office door, try installing a door sweep, such as Suptikes’ Huge Gap door draft stopper.

Recent findings suggest that for renters who aren’t allowed to attach anything to a door, roll up a towel and use it to block the under-door gap to reduce noise transfer. Commercial products are also available, such as the Sunolga draft stopper, and they often come with loops on the ends to hang the item on a door knob when not in use.

It has been revealed that trying to focus on work when the kids are playing in the room overhead is challenging at best, virtually impossible at worst. Reducing noise transfer through a ceiling can be accomplished by soundproofing the floor of the room that lies overhead. For those who live in an apartment and don’t have access to the room above, noise-dampening methods are limited.

Homeowners can sandwich a layer of MLV between the existing ceiling drywall and then hang a second layer of drywall. Unlike the MLV method mentioned above to soundproof walls, the simplest way to install MLV overhead is to cut and attach it first to the new drywall panels and then install the panels. Since MLV is heavy, a drywall lift will be necessary for raising the panels.

In a rented apartment, fewer good options are available. Still, renters can reduce ceiling sound transfer using ultra-lightweight foam boards, such as UCreate foamboard. Attach the boards to the ceiling with removable mounting putty, such as Gorilla Mounting Putty, that won’t harm the ceiling.

Soundproofing floors by reducing noise transfer from a room below is relatively easy by carpeting the floor or covering hard flooring with one or more large area rugs. When used in combination with the other soundproofing techniques, this may be enough to dampen most noises to a tolerable level.

Homeowners may want to soundproof the ceiling of the room below (described previously) for additional noise reduction.

Renters typically cannot structurally modify floors or ceilings, so if adding rugs isn’t sufficient, consider covering hard flooring with a layer of cork, such as Corksidol’s ½-inch-thick cork tiles, to help absorb sound. A large area rug can be added over the cork to protect it and offer a finished look.

Sources indicate that water hammer is the product of hydraulic shock, and it can be loud enough to startle anyone who isn’t expecting it. Water hammer occurs when the water is shut off abruptly, and the water supply pipe reacts by jerking and bumping into other pipes or framing members in walls or floors.

According to recent reports, if you have access to the offending pipes, slipping some foam pipe insulation around them, such as Foam King Brand foam pipe insulation, will usually stop the problem. Alternatively, a plumber can install a water hammer arrester, such as the Sioux Chief water hammer arrester, to keep the pipe from jerking when the water is turned off.

In a recent development, hard objects, such as metal and solid wood tables and chairs, do not absorb sound so that noise can bounce around a room. Swapping hard chairs for upholstered chairs and overstuffed sofas will help dampen sound waves and keep them from echoing in the room.

According to recent reports, additionally, following beneficial feng shui practices can also help block noise. Feng shui is a Chinese system of orienting rooms and adding features in a harmonious and pleasing manner. By adding a water feature, the trickling sound of the water will help distract from background noises, and placing live plants throughout the room will help absorb sound while freshening the air.

Industry observers note that effective soundproofing involves using a combination of techniques to block sound transfer from outside a room while absorbing sounds inside the room. The best time to soundproof a home (or room) is during construction, when the walls and floors can be framed in a manner to reduce sound transfer, but unwanted noises can be significantly stifled in existing homes too.

In general, products and materials that are dense and soft will absorb the most noise, including MLV, carpeting, cork, and curtains. Whether you own or rent your home, you don’t have to live with distracting sounds. Learning how to make a room soundproof goes a long way toward maintaining a comfortable living space.

Real egg cartons are not used to block sound. Rather, egg carton-shaped foam, such as Jdejiela‘s egg crate panels, are used to line walls to dampen noise.

The best sound-blocking materials are dense and soft, such as foam and carpeting.

The most effective way is during new construction by utilizing staggered wall studs and joists to create a dead-air space that reduces sound transfer.

Yes, but making a room completely soundproof involves specialized construction practices that create dead-air spaces in floors and walls. Sound reduction is what most are going for.

Industry observers note that while bubbling or gurgling is a relatively common toilet problem, it’s not an concern you want to ignore. When a toilet bubbles, it indicates that negative air pressure (suction) is building up in the drain line, creating an airlock of sorts. Most likely this buildup of air is due to a clog.

Depending on the severity of the clog, you may be able to clear it yourself with a plunger or an eco-friendly Drano alternative. Otherwise, you might have to call a plumber. Is a gurgling toilet dangerous? Not typically, but if the culprit is a broken or collapsed sewer line, it will have to be fixed, and the sooner the better. If the job is put off, waste could back up into toilets, showers, or tubs. The following guide will help you get to the root of toilet bubbling, and offer solutions to the problem.

In a recent development, clogs typically occur in one of two areas: somewhere in the drain system, which could be close to the toilet or farther down the main sewer line that connects to your community’s sewer system, or in your home’s vent stack (the pipe that allows sewer gasses to escape through the roof). To fix the gurgling toilet once and for all, you’ll need to identify the location of the clog and take steps to remove it.

Recent findings suggest that ridgid’s Power Spin+ has an easy-to-use pull trigger and handle; can be attached to a power drill to dislodge serious blockages. Read the review.

It has been revealed that addressing clogs is key to fixing air bubbles in your toilet—but not all clogs are created equal. A few troubleshooting steps can help you identify whether the solution is DIY-friendly, or if it’s time to call a plumber.

Industry observers note that if the cause of the gurgling is in the drainpipe, simply plunging the toilet might create enough pressure to dislodge a light-to-moderate clog. Bathroom fixtures (tub, sink, shower) often connect to the same drain line that runs from the toilet, so you’ll want to seal off these drains with duct tape before plunging. If you plunge without sealing the drains, the pressure plunging creates can escape through other drain fixtures instead of dislodging the clog.

Sources indicate that start by selecting the right plunger, such as the JS Jackson accordion-style plunger, which was a top pick in our researched guide to the best plungers. With the toilet bowl full of water, fit the head of the plunger tightly to the drain hole in the bottom of the bowl. Try to dislodge the clog with 10 to 15 firm pumping motions, then wait to see if the toilet gurgles again. If you don’t have a plunger handy, other ways of unclogging a toilet without one may be just as effective. However, if the gurgling continues, move on to the following steps.

A sewer snake (also known as a plumber’s snake or plumber’s auger) can often remove tough clogs in a drainpipe that plunging can’t manage. Featuring a long cable and a head with cutting blades for chopping through stubborn clogs, the best drain snakes may even have a manual or motorized crank.

If you’re not sure how to snake a toilet, a manual toilet auger ($25 to $100 at home-improvement stores) is inserted into the toilet bowl. As you turn the crank, the head works its way down the drainpipe, cutting through clogs. This type of auger is limited to the distance of its cable reach, generally 5 to 15 feet.

It has been revealed that if a clog is so deep in the drainpipe that a small sewer snake cannot reach it, you can upgrade to a motorized auger that will reach 50+ feet, or rent a medium-sized drain cleaner from a home improvement store. Renting the equipment for an afternoon might run you $40 to $50, whereas calling a plumber to snake the drain could run you $150 to $300. Additional repairs, such as removing tree roots from a sewer line or fixing a broken sewer line, may be even costlier.

Since the auger head on a motorized sewer snake is often too large to wind its way through the toilet bowl, the toilet should be removed from its base and the auger inserted into the drainpipe at floor level. When the machine is turned on, the auger will work its way down the line, its razor-sharp blades cutting through tough clogs.

For clogs even deeper in the sewer line—as far out as the middle of your yard—you’ll want to auger the lines from the sewer cleanout, which is just outside of your home, directly over the sewer pipe. To locate the cleanout, check your basement or crawlspace to see where the main sewer line exits your house. Many cleanout pipes extend a few inches above the ground and feature a large PVC cap, but others may terminate just below ground level. You may need to do a little digging to uncover it. Once you’ve removed the cap from the cleanout pipe with an adjustable wrench, auger the sewer line from there. If the toilet gurgling stops, you’ve successfully removed the sewer clog that caused it; if the sounds continue, try troubleshooting the vent stack.

Checking and clearing the vent stack requires getting on the roof, so if you’re not completely comfortable with that, be safe and call the pros. Here’s how to check the vent stack yourself:.

Vent clogs are often caused by leaves and debris, or even the carcass of a small animal that got stuck in the pipe. If the clog is within a few feet of the top of the pipe, you may be able to remove it with a straightened-out wire coat hanger or a toilet brush. Deeper clogs can often be removed by running water from a garden hose in the pipe, which can dislodge the clog, washing it down the pipe and out through the sewer.

It has been revealed that can a gurgling toilet fix itself? Unfortunately, the answer is no. If the troubleshooting methods above failed to silence your gurgling toilet bowl, it’s time to call the plumber. Plumbers have specialized emergency plumbing tools and equipment, such as powerful sewer augers that can chop through anything blocking the main sewer line.

According to recent reports, according to Roto-Rooter, gurgling toilets can also indicate that tree roots have grown into the sewer line. If this is the case, repairs are best left to a professional plumber. Professionals can use mini cameras that drop into vent stacks to locate the source of the problem. There’s also a slim chance that the main sewer line in your yard has broken or collapsed, in which case excavation and professional repairs might be necessary.

#113193. Industry News: "Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press": "Ambiguous Evidence: Enjoining Repetition of Libels"

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1293 w)

Industry News: "Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press": "Ambiguous Evidence: Enjoining Repetition of Libels"

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1293 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I'm serializing my new Notre Dame Law Review article, "Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press: Some Illustrative Examples"; here's the third and last Part:.
  • It has been revealed that throughout much of American history, the dominant view has been that courts can't enjoin libels.
  • Sources indicate that yet since then, many state courts have allowed permanent injunctions against libels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I'm serializing my new Notre Dame Law Review article, "Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press: Some Illustrative Examples"; here's the third and last Part:.

It has been revealed that throughout much of American history, the dominant view has been that courts can't enjoin libels. The first precedent on this was Brandreth v. Lance (1839), an 1839 New York trial court decision. This was followed by State ex rel. Liversey v. Judge (1882), an 1882 Louisiana Supreme Court decision. Subsequent decisions helped establish this as a firm rule, seemingly culminating in Near v. Minnesota ex rel. Olson.

Sources indicate that yet since then, many state courts have allowed permanent injunctions against libels. By my count the court systems of thirty-four states have either so held or have in practice been so acting, with only six states plus D.C. continuing to categorically bar such injunctions. {See Eugene Volokh, Anti-Libel Injunctions, 168 U. Pa. L. Rev. 73 (2019).}.

Recent findings suggest that this trend seems to have accelerated with the rise of the internet. Historically, a libel has been a short, sharp shock—typically, a one-time article in a newspaper that is printed and can't be removed—with the only possible remedy being damages or criminal prosecution. But the internet can turn libel into a steady drip, drip, drip of damage, with more readers seeing a libelous web page every day. Injunctions thus seem a more useful remedy.

The internet also makes it easier for judgment-proof defendants to cause real damage; an injunction can thus be useful in a way that a damages remedy might not be. Criminal libel is theoretically available in about ten states, and there are indeed likely a couple of dozen criminal libel prosecutions in the United States each year. But in most states the only way to deploy criminal remedies in service of protecting reputation is through getting an injunction that can be enforced through the threat of criminal contempt.

It has been revealed that are these injunctions contrary to the original meaning of the First Amendment? The answer turns out to be complicated, especially if we focus on permanent injunctions, entered to forbid the repetition of material found to be libelous in a final judgment (with the defendant having had an opportunity to call for a jury trial).

It's true that early sources often view the freedom of the press as precluding prior restraints: To quote William Blackstone, "The liberty of the press is indeed essential to the nature of a free state: but this consists in laying no previous restraints upon publications, and not in freedom from censure for criminal matter when published." Yet this doesn't quite speak to the modern question whether the law may restrain repetition of material for matter found to be criminal (or tortious).

According to recent reports, nor does it speak to whether the law may require removal of such matter after a trial: Removal just wasn't practically an option in the print era. In such situations of injunctions against repetition of an already published libel or ordering its removal, "[e]very freeman" would retain the "undoubted right to lay what sentiments he pleases before the public" (again quoting Blackstone) at least in the first instance.

Nor is there a "restrictive power of a licenser" or "control of an inspector" in the sense that the Framers likely understood licensers, which is to say officials administering a licensing system. (To quote St. George Tucker, under that system "all books printed were previously licensed by some of the great offices of state, or the two universities, and all foreign books were exposed to a similar scrutiny before they were vended.") The injunction is imposed by a judge, often following a jury verdict, administering justice between two parties, not running a traditional licensing system that "subject[s] all freedom of sentiment to the prejudices of one man, and make[s] him the arbitrary and infallible judge of all controverted points in learning, religion, and government.".

In a recent development, likewise, early sources stressed the importance of allowing a jury to resolve what is true and false in libel cases. But, as I noted, the modern permanent injunction in libel cases is entered after a final judgment on the merits, which at least in principle allows a defendant to demand a jury trial. If the defendant has so demanded, then any injunction would be based on the jury verdict.

This stems in part from the twentieth-century merger of law and equity, since equitable remedies, such as injunctions, can now be issued following the use of the legal procedure of a jury trial. (Historically, one argument against injunctions in libel cases has been that "equity will not enjoin a libel," a statement about the limits of the equity courts more than about constitutional protections for free expression.) Indeed, the Delaware Court of Chancery, which operates in a state system where law and equity remain largely separate, has continued to hold that it generally can't enjoin libel. But it expressly left open the possibility that, once the Delaware Superior Court (the law court) concludes—after a jury trial, if the parties don't choose a bench trial—that a statement is libelous, an injunction can then be issued.

According to recent reports, in practice, anti-libel injunctions are often parts of default judgments, or follow bench trials, and thus don't involve factual findings by juries. In both those situations, though, the defendant can be remarked to have waived his right to a jury trial. To be sure, temporary restraining orders and preliminary injunctions are entered before any opportunity for a jury trial—but for that reason many courts continue to reject them on First Amendment grounds.

And, as the California Supreme Court held in allowing such post-final-judgment permanent injunctions, the reasoning of Near v. Minnesota ex rel. Olson expressly sets aside injunctions in traditional civil libel disputes:.

Industry observers note that the high court was careful to point out … that the statute being considered was "not aimed at the redress of individual or private wrongs. Remedies for libel remain available and unaffected." … But most significant is that the court … clarified that it was not addressing "questions as to the extent of authority to prevent publications in order to protect private rights according to the principles governing the exercise of the jurisdiction of courts of equity." In a footnote, the court cited [an] … article by Roscoe Pound that observed that English courts permit "an injunction in case the libel was repeated or publication was continued after a jury had found the matter libelous." Therefore, Near expressly did not address the problem posed in the present case.

Industry observers note that the Supreme Court hasn't confronted such permanent injunctions against repetition of proven libel since Near, but it has authorized injunctions against obscenity (which Near had anticipated) and against commercial speech that proposes illegal transactions. The one case in which it granted certiorari as to anti-libel injunctions, Tory v. Cochran (2005), largely disappeared when the plaintiff, famed lawyer Johnnie Cochran, died while the case was pending. None of these cases discussed the original meaning of the First Amendment, and the lower court cases dealing with the matter have largely not discussed it, either.

Recent findings suggest that so here we have a fairly rich body of originalist evidence related to libel law generally. We have a considerable body of evidence from before and shortly after the Framing that talks about "previous restraints." And we have some nineteenth-century sources that seem to take the view that all injunctions in libel cases are unconstitutional. But how exactly do the Framing-era sources apply to a permanent anti-libel injunction issued by a court following the resolution of a libel case? Hard to know for sure.

When temperatures drop, working outdoors can become downright uncomfortable, and that’s where a heated vest can come in handy. Will they survive snow, rain, or sleet? We put these vests through their paces, tested all of their functions, and noted how long they stayed warm on a single battery charge.

Moving freely is essential in many outdoor occupations, including construction, surveying, and landscaping, so piling on constricting clothing layers isn’t usually an option. And, as our top pick, the Ororo Men’s Lightweight Heated Vest, demonstrated, they’re far more comfortable than you might imagine.

When we tested the following heated vests, the outdoor temperature ranged from 25 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit during the day, dropping into single digits overnight. With the addition of high winds on some days, the wind chill hovered around 0 degrees Fahrenheit, so we had plenty of opportunities to enjoy the warmth the vests provided.

The following heated vests feature varying levels of heat distribution, ease of use, functionality, and comfort. Battery runtime was tested at the highest temperature—you can reasonably expect two to three times longer heating on lower settings.

We’ve been working on replacing our outdoor pergola before the snow falls, but the temperatures have dipped down into the teens, so having a heated vest like this one to wear under regular clothing has been ideal.
